News.title: 'I've been homeless for years - the PM must tackle cost of living crisis to end plight of thousands'
News.content:
'I've been homeless for years - the PM must tackle cost of living crisis to end plight of thousands'

Ivan Corbett, 37, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham today in Elswick, Newcastle, where he revealed his alcohol and cocaine addiction had plunged him £2,000 into debt

View 2 Images Ivan Corbett met the Prime Minister to discuss the problem of homelessness which has impacted his life for years (Image: Andy Commins)

Desperate Ivan Corbett has spent years sofa-surfing after his life was gripped by alcohol and drug problems.

But the 37-year-old says his meeting with Andy Burnham has filled him with hope that the new Prime Minister can tackle the homelessness problem. He says the Labour Government must address the crippling cost of living crisis that is pushing people into debt and poverty.

Speaking after his meeting with Mr Burnham at the Changing Lives homeless shelter in Elswick, Newcastle, Ivan said: “He just wants to get everyone off the streets. I’m hopeful he can do that. But he needs to address other stuff too. Council tax, all the builds you need to pay. Some people just can’t afford it. It’s the cost of living crisis and the problems with universal credit, they’re putting people into debt.”

View 2 Images Ivan urged the PM to tackle rising bills which are pushing people into debt and forcing them from their homes (Image: Andy Commins)

Ivan, originally from Scotswood, Newcastle, lost his home in 2022 after a dispute with his landlord. He came home to find the locks changed and his possessions gone. He has been drifting between homes, unable to find employment since, all while battling addiction that saw him spiral into debt. His story is echoed across the North East, which has seen a 39% rise in rough sleeping.

Ivan said: “The landlord changed the locks and I couldn’t get back in the property. All my possessions were locked inside, I lost it all. I’ve just been sofa surfing since then. I haven’t been able to work, but hen I do it’s just cash-in-hand jobs. I’ve been going to soup kitchens and food banks. I’ve just had to survive."

Ivan was consumed by a cocaine addiction which saw him accumulate a drugs debt totalling more than £2,000. His friends were forced to step in and pay off dealers who threatened to harm him if he didn't settle the payment.

He said: “If I didn’t pay they’d break my legs.” Ivan explained: “I’ve got a problem with alcohol - when I start drinking spirits I can’t stop. But I’ve also got a cocaine problem. I got into debts over cocaine and a friend had to pay my debt. It’s slowly coming down. I knew I had to pay - it’s not worth getting your legs broken over a debt.”

Speaking about his problems, Ivan said: “I’m alright now. Sometimes I can’t get out of bed because I’ve got depression and anxiety. But I’m doing OK.”

Ivan spoke out as Mr Burnham pledged an additional £102 million to help local authorities get people off the streets for Christmas. He issued a "rallying call" to solve the problem, but admitted Government money alone may not be enough to solve the problem.

The former Manchester mayor said he feels "very passionately" about tackling homelessness but indicated that wider society including community and faith organisations must play their part. His pledge includes an £8.4 million boost to the Ending Homelessness in Communities Fund, in recognition of the work of charities, faith groups and community organisations in the sector.

In the West End of Newcastle - where Mr Burnham today met service users and support workers - there are more than a dozen homeless shelters trying to tackle the problem.

Article continues below

The area is home to some of the most deprived communities in the region – with 46% of children in Elswick, 42% in Arthur’s Hill and the city centre, and 38% in Benwell living below the breadline, according to official Government figures for 2022/23.

News.title: Monzo down - live: Banking app users 'can't transfer money' as thousands report problems
News.content:
Thousands of Monzo customers are reporting problems with the app and bank transfers as outage reports surge across the UK.

Thousands of Monzo customers are reporting problems with the company's banking app and bank transfers as an outage hits users this afternoon.

Downdetector, an independent website that monitors outages, recorded 3,195 reports at 1.05pm on August 19 of issues with Monzo, compared with a usual baseline of zero.

Customers have taken to X to complain about the disruption, with one person asking: "Is the app down - trying to transfer money but it isn't leaving my account?"

Monzo acknowledged the issues in a response, saying: "We're sorry for any trouble you're having making bank transfers or using the Monzo app. Our team is aware of the issue and working on a fix to get things running again ASAP. Thanks for bearing with us, we appreciate your patience." The cause of the disruption has not yet been confirmed.

News.title: Shoreham sea tragedy prompts son of drowning victim to call for water safety minister
News.content:
Shoreham sea tragedy prompts son of drowning victim to call for water safety minister

The latest drowning tragedy to hit the UK this year has prompted calls for a meeting with the PM and the appointment of a water safety minister to stop the drowning 'epidemic'

View 5 Images Robbie Jones, whose dad drowned, is urging the PM to appoint a water safety minister urgently (Image: Supplied)

A son whose dad drowned in the sea off Hove in East Sussex, is urging the Prime Minister to appoint a water safety minister urgently after another ‘terrible’ and 'gut-wrenching' tragedy struck just minutes away from their home.

‌



Three members of the same family, a couple and their teenage daughter, died after getting into difficulty in the sea at Shoreham. A younger girl is also in hospital critical. Coastguard helicopters, ambulances and police were scrambled to the coastal town in West Sussex on Tuesday afternoon following reports that four people were in trouble in the water. It's thought the family were camping nearby. They entered the water for a group swim in the harbour, Sussex Police said.

‌



“This is a really shocking incident and it brings it all back very vividly,” Robbie Jones, now 30, whose dad died in the sea 14 minutes along the coast, told the Mirror. Robbie, who supports The Mirror’s ‘Save Lives for Sam’ campaign, has told how it took less than a minute for his dad Gareth Jones, 69, to drown after going into the sea to save the family's young cockapoo, Connie. Since the tragedy in 2021, his son has become a water safety advocate visiting schools to spread the message.

‌



View 5 Images Robbie with his dad Gareth who drowned along the same coast as the recent triple tragedy (Image: supplied)

Shoreham: Police confirm three dead in waters off Sussex coast

Horror as bodies of three family members pulled from sea while young girl fights for life READ MORE :

But after this latest horrifying tragedy at sea, he is asking to meet Andy Burnham and says of the Labour leader’s support of our campaign: “Words won’t save people’s lives - actions will, Prime Minister”.

‌



He pointed out the PM recently appointed Baroness Blake of Leeds as fire minister, serving in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, to tackle wildfires blazing across the country. He says he also needs to appoint a water safety minister, a role which could be added to Angela Rayner’s brief.

5 View 5 Images The Mirror's Save Lives for Sam campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer. 5 View 5 Images The Save Lives for Sam water safety demands urging the Government to make changes

‌



The Mirror has been calling for a water safety minister since we launched our 'Save Lives for Sam' campaign earlier this year, to stop the “catastrophic” deaths of 33 children who drown in England every year - the equivalent of a classroom of children lost. We told how campaigners were warning drowning in the UK has become an "epidemic" and a "national emergency."

Our campaign has been backed by bereaved families, the RNLI, The Royal Life Saving Society UK (RLSS UK), RoSPA (the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents), Lee Pitcher MP, the Black Swimming Association (BSA), The National Water Safety Forum, Swim England and The Swimming Alliance and Olympic legends including Becky Adlington.

Robbie said: “I would like to arrange a meeting, let’s get something done here. Let’s not have another year like this, many of these drownings, if not all of them, were totally avoidable and many of them happening to our young people.

‌



“We need real action. I know Andy Burnham is a decent guy. I had a few weeks work experience with him at Westminster when I was 18 years old. And I know he’s a really generous and compassionate guy

“It was gut-wrenching last night when I heard the news come through. When you hear of the tragedy and all being from the same family, it hit me hard, it’s horrible news. We had one drowning in one family and to have three in one family is unimaginable.

"It makes me feel like I’m failing in my duty. Five and a half years ago I started trying to get the message out about water safety but the numbers are going the wrong way.

‌



“It makes me feel like I’ve got to redouble my efforts. It brought it all back, I have memories of playing in Shoreham and its regarded as a pretty safe beach and this is a reminder that it can happen in any circumstances very quickly. The tide and conditions can turn.

View 5 Images Robbie says dads die, but not from drowning (Image: Supplied)

“It would have been my dad’s birthday on Friday. He would have been 75 and he should still be here. I feel robbed not having here to have a pint with him. I don’t want anyone to have the same tragedy as I have, would not wish it on my worst enemies. Dads die but they don’t drown, it’s hard dealing with the grief.

Article continues below

“We need someone dedicated to water safety in this country It’s not just the summer this happens, my dad obviously drowned in January. Accidental drownings happen when it’s not high season. It's not just just people living by the coast."

A national strategy to address the “public health disaster” of drowning was launched in England last month. Among the measures being considered are: providing every child in England with water safety education and swimming lessons; establishing how climate change can increase risks; and media campaigns to inform bystanders how to respond to a potential drowning.

Speaking at the announcement of the strategy in Canary Wharf, east London, on Thursday, Prof Mike Tipton, the chair of Water Safety England, said the measures would “eradicate the scourge of drowning”. He added: “Drowning is an ongoing public health disaster that, despite claiming more lives than fire, flooding, or knife crime, often stays below the radar.”

News.title: Man falls to his death from top of building in Edinburgh city centre
News.content:
Man falls to his death from top of building in Edinburgh city centre

Police in Edinburgh received a report of a man having fallen from height at a building in St Andrew Square this morning - he was sadly pronounced dead shortly after

View Image Emergency services at the scene in Edinburgh today (Image: Edinburgh Live)

A man has sadly died after falling from the top of a building in the city centre of Edinburgh.

‌



The incident took place at around 11.30am today. St Andrew Square was cordoned off and a large green tarpaulin was erected at the entrance to Harvey Nichols, which closed following the incident.

‌



Officers could be seen around the cordon, speaking to members of the public, while two ambulances were parked up outside the department store, Edinburgh Live reports.

‌



Police said they received a report of a man having fallen from height at a building in St Andrew Square. He was pronounced dead shortly afterwards.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Around 11.35am on Wednesday, 19 August, 2026, we were called to a report that a man had fallen from height at a building in the St Andrew Square area of Edinburgh.

Article continues below

“Emergency services attended however the man was pronounced dead a short time later. Enquiries are ongoing.”

Lothian Buses has also diverted two services from the area as emergency services remain at the scene. Both the CS1 and ET1 have been rerouted for the time being.

News.title: Shoreham deaths - latest: Father among three pulled from sea was Palestinian refugee
News.content:
Three members of the same family died after getting into difficulty in the water at Shoreham-by-Sea in Sussex - while a young girl from the family is now fighting for her life

The father who was one of three family members pulled dead from the water at Shoreham-by-Sea has been named as Palestinian refugee Hossam Al-Khawas.

Three people from the same family - a man, Hossam, a woman, and a teenage girl - tragically died they got into trouble in the sea, sparking a massive emergency services response.

A fourth person, a younger girl from the same family, also got into difficulty but was pulled from the sea and remains in a critical condition in hospital. Eyewitnesses claim one of the children involved in a tragic incident in the water off Shoreham-by-Sea had become trapped in a fishing net.

Local landscaper Joe Chrisp, 24, said: "It happened when I was on my way back from work. There were loads of police, and I got turned around. It’s so tragic. One of the kids apparently got caught in a fishing net."

It's thought the family were camping near the scene and had entered the water for a group swim in the harbour, Sussex Police said.

People living in the area say Shoreham Harbour has a steep shelf, where the seabed drops away quickly. It can make it difficult for swimmers to keep their balance, they say. Mr Al-Khawas's name was confirmed by the Palestinian Embassy but it was unable to confirm the names of the other family members.

The tragic deaths in Shoreham today come as the Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Kenya helicopter crash: 6 dead as safari 'tourist' chopper crashes in Samburu
News.content:
Six people have been killed after a safari helicopter crashed near Mt Ololokwe in Kenya’s Samburu County, with tourists reportedly on board

A helicopter has crashed near Kirish close to Mt Ololokwe in Kenya’s Samburu County, with all six people on board dead.

A preliminary police report cited by Kenyan newspaper The Star suggested tourists were travelling in the aircraft, although their nationalities have not yet been established and this has not been confirmed.

Local residents and rescue teams were heading towards the scene, where smoke and fire had been seen following the crash.

The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority said the helicopter had been travelling towards the Ewaso Nyiro river, which runs through the Samburu National Reserve, shortly after 9am local time.

The helicopter was operated by local safari company Tropic Air and crashed in the foothills Mt Ololokwe, local media reports.

News.title: TV doctor calls on government to take action on life expectancy gap across UK
News.content:
TV doctor calls on government to take action on life expectancy gap across UK

TV Doctor Amir Khan has called on the Government to end 'postcode inequality' in healthcare.

Dr Amir Khan shines a light on the 'postcode lottery' of life expectancy

Dr Amir Khan, a media medic and author, has described life expectancy disparities as a 'national crisis' after it emerged those living in affluent places like Marylebone and Berkhamsted are living up to 18 years longer than those in generally poorer areas like Blackpool and Glasgow.

‌



The life expectancy figures in the activation comes from analysis of an ONS report on 'health state life expectancy estimates' for those born in England between 2019 and 2023. They were calculated from key criteria including housing quality, air pollution, financial pressures and local living conditions - all believed to significantly influence how long someone lives.

‌



View 4 Images The installation was held in Old Spitalfields Market (Image: PinPep)

‌



Having been raised himself in a working-class inner-city area of Bradford, Dr Khan argued "health (care) starts long before someone walks into a GP surgery".

The TV doctor, who has teamed with Health Equals, a campaigning coalition group aiming to improve health equality opportunities across the UK, added: “I don't just see the impact of health inequalities in my work as a GP, I've lived them too.

“Today, I see these same challenges affecting many of my patients. I see people living in damp homes, struggling with financial insecurity or juggling multiple jobs, and I see the impact that can have on their health.”

‌



He unveiled a 'traffic-stopping' ‘Shelf Life’ installation in Old Spitalfields Market in East London to draw attention to the campaign group's work.

The display featured oversized supermarket-style packaging showing reduced ‘expiry dates’ based on life expectancy figures from different parts of the country, highlighting how some people are effectively losing years off their life.

View 4 Images Almost all of the people polled said the life expectancy differences is a problem (Image: PinPep)

‌



He said: “We're very good at treating illness, it is shaped by things like our homes, jobs, education and local environment. Your postcode shouldn't determine your shelf life. But right now, in the UK, it does.

“That's why these figures should be considered a national crisis, and why we need governments to commit to meaningful action to tackle the root causes of poor health and health inequalities.”

Life spans in more affluent areas like Marylebone and Berkhamsted are estimated to be up to 88 years of age - 18 years more than they are in areas like Glasgow and Grimsby, where 70 is the average.

‌



In a poll of 2,000 adults, also commissioned by Health Equals, it emerged almost all appear to share Dr Khan’s concerns - 95% agreed the difference in life expectancy across the UK is a problem.

The most significant factors influencing lifespan are education (65%), access to transport (57%) and access to affordable healthy food (92%), according to respondents.

View 4 Images Will Mellor and Dr Amir Khan are supporting Health Equals' campaign (Image: PinPep)

‌



Actor and TV presenter, Will Mellor, who is also supporting the campaign, added: “It's shocking to think that there's an 18-year gap in life expectancy between some communities across the UK.

“Having grown up on a council estate in Stockport, that’s difficult to get my head around. Two people from different parts of the UK can be working hard, doing their best, and yet one could still live so many years fewer than the other.

“What really struck me about this campaign is seeing the data broken down to such a local level. It stops being just a set of statistics and becomes about the places we live, work and raise our families.

‌



“I'd encourage everyone to check their own postcode on the Health Equals website because the results are genuinely eye-opening.

“When you see the difference between communities that can be just a few miles apart, the issue becomes impossible to ignore.”

View 4 Images Places like Glasgow and Grimsby have a lower life expectancy (Image: PinPep)

‌



Of those who took part in the study by OnePoll.com, only two in 10 think that the government is doing enough to help reduce inequalities in health between people in different postcodes in the UK.

Paul McDonald, director of Health Equals, which is calling on our new Prime Minister to change the law to make it a legal duty to create better health in every postal area, added: “Let’s not forget that behind these figures are real people with families, loved ones, jobs, hobbies, and their lives are being cut short because of things out of their control - this should be considered a national crisis.

“This isn’t just bad luck or down to individual choices, it's because too many people don’t have access to the basics that help us stay healthy. And these inequalities don’t just affect individuals, they hold back families, jobs and our economy, and put pressure on services like the NHS.

Article continues below

"Our health should be a national priority, and change is possible. We are calling for a change in the law to make improving health and tackling inequalities a legal duty for this and future governments. If Andy Burnham is serious about creating good growth in every British postcode, this will be one of his first priorities in Number 10.”

News.title: Sleep better and feel calmer with Lidl £5 Special Buy coming out this Thursday
News.content:
Sleep better and feel calmer with Lidl £5 Special Buy coming out this Thursday

Shoppers could take advantage of the £5 Special Buy deal to potentially improve their mood and sleep quality

View 3 Images Shoppers don't have long to wait as the new offer comes out Thursday (stock image) (Image: Getty)

Lidl is introducing a new selection of Special Buys this week. One particular item is likely to be of interest not only to gardeners but also to anyone who would like to potentially sleep better and feel calmer.

‌



On Thursday, August 20, Lidl is releasing a variety of Middle Aisle offers, including a range of flowers and plants. Shoppers will be able to get their hands on pots of cyclamen, celosia, calathea and ornamental grass. Customers will also be able to buy a pack of potted lavender for £4.99.

‌



In the product description, Lidl says: "Perfect for attracting bees and butterflies. Plant in pots or borders. Height: 16-20cm. Six pack."

‌



Beyond its striking purple blossoms, lavender has been celebrated for centuries for its profound therapeutic benefits. For those struggling to unwind, research suggests the soothing fragrance of lavender acts as a natural remedy for stress and anxiety.

Using lavender in aromatherapy can help soothe the nervous system and boost your mood. However, it's more effective as a supportive tool rather than a treatment for serious anxiety disorders.

View 3 Images Lidl shoppers can buy a six-pack of lavender for £4.99 from Thursday (Image: Lidl)

‌



Lavender is a plant with many uses. It is commonly used in several forms to promote health and wellness, including dried flowers, essential oils, topical oils, capsules, teas, tisanes, infusions, creams, lotions, salves, and beauty products.

A comprehensive meta-analysis conducted in 2019 revealed that people with anxiety disorders who consumed 160-milligram lavender oil capsules saw notable reductions in their anxiety levels. Similar findings have been reported in other studies. For instance, a 2015 study included 60 participants in a coronary intensive care unit. The researchers discovered that those who received lavender essential oil treatment experienced reduced anxiety and improved sleep quality.

Scientific research shows that inhaling lavender can lower heart rate and blood pressure, shifting the nervous system into a relaxed state. The plant is also one of the most trusted natural sleep aids available.

‌



View 3 Images Lavender has been used for its health properties for centuries (stock image)

Incorporating lavender into your evening routine—whether by placing a potted plant in the bedroom or using it as aromatherapy—has been shown to enhance sleep quality. Research shows it can help people fall asleep faster and increase the duration of deep sleep, ensuring you wake up feeling truly refreshed.

A study from 2015 found that people who used lavender aromatherapy reported feeling more refreshed when they woke up. Additionally, a 2010 study involving people with anxiety disorders showed that taking lavender oil by mouth helped them sleep for a longer duration at night.

Article continues below

The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) recommends planting lavender in a sunny area that receives plenty of light, in soil that drains well and is neutral to alkaline. It stresses the importance of avoiding soggy winter soils and dense shade, and suggests pruning right after the flowers fade in late summer to keep the plant from becoming leggy. It's important to avoid cutting into old, bare wood.

News.title: Thunderstorm warnings issued for parts of UK with flash flooding expected
News.content:
Yellow thunderstorm warnings have been issued across the UK, with heavy showers expected to lead to flash flooding and travel disruption.

The Met Office warnings will come into force across northern England, Northern Ireland and eastern Scotland later in the day on Wednesday. The warning for northern England will remain in place until Thursday morning.

The downpours follow almost two months of dry weather, with parts of the country experiencing their first rain in weeks on Tuesday.

People in areas impacted by thunderstorms have been told by the Met Office to expect that businesses and homes could flood, transport services could be delayed and power cuts are likely.

The yellow weather warnings are in place for:

Northern Ireland from 12:00 until 23:59 BST on Wednesday

Parts of North East Scotland, including Aberdeen, from 14:00 until 21:00 on Wednesday

Parts of the North of England, including Manchester and Newcastle upon Tyne, from 19:00 until 10:00 on Thursday

The Met Office said lightning, hail and thunder were expected in the areas affected by warnings, with up to 30mm of rain expected within a few hours in parts of North East Scotland and across Northern Ireland.

Parts of northern England could see up to 50mm of rain within six hours.

Much of the UK has seen a mixture of sunshine and scattered showers already on Wednesday.

In Wisley, Surrey, a 62-day long dry spell was broken on Wednesday morning, with the remarkable run ending after 1.6mm fell before 10.00.

News.title: Jump in energy bills drives UK inflation to highest rate for four months
News.content:
Higher energy bills drove UK inflation up to 2.9% in the year to July, the highest level in four months, according to new figures.

Gas prices soared at the sharpest pace in almost four years, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, leading to an increase in the cap on household energy bills in July. Energy costs surged after US-Israel war with Iran began, which has restricted global oil supplies.

July's reading is the highest since March but some price growth slowed. Food inflation, at 1.3%, is at its lowest rate for close to five years.

Experts said the inflation figure is unlikely to influence the Bank of England to change its key interest rate at its next meeting in September.

Energy costs for households rose on 1 July after Ofgem, the energy regulator, increased the price cap on gas and electricity costs by 13%, which added Â£221 a year to the typical bill.

Homes are forecast to see a 4% rise in energy bills from October, according to Cornwall Insight, which would take them to the highest level since July 2023.

Therre is ongoing uncertainty over the US-Iran conflict, which has seen effective closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key trading passage for ships carrying oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities.

Cornwall Insight, an independent energy consultancy, added that energy price pressures were being compounded by the ongoing heatwave across Europe "increasing gas demand for power generation to meeting air conditioning and cooling demand".

News.title: Tennis player Nick Kyrgios suspended after testing positive for cocaine
News.content:
Nick Kyrgios has been provisionally suspended from tennis after testing positive for cocaine.

The Australian submitted a sample during the Mallorca Open on 22 June that was later found to contain benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine.

Former world number 13 Kyrgios has been provisionally suspended, external since 4 August.

The International Tennis Integrity Agency said Kyrgios could appeal against the provisional suspension "but has not done so to date".

In a post on Instagram, Kyrgios said he made "a huge mistake" and takes "full responsibility" for it.

Under the suspension, Kyrgios cannot play, coach at or attend Grand Slams or any events sanctioned by the men's and women's tennis tours pending the outcome of a tribunal.

Kyrgios could be banned for up to four years - but if he can prove he took the drug outside of a competition, the maximum ban he would face is three months.

The 31-year-old has played just four singles matches this season, having struggled with knee and wrist injuries in recent years.

He last played in the men's doubles at Wimbledon, where he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.

News.title: PM unveils plan to get rough sleepers off streets for Christmas
News.content:
Every rough sleeper in England will be offered accommodation this winter, the prime minister has said.

Andy Burnham made ending rough sleeping his first pledge when entering Downing Street in July and now says he wants "to get everyone in for Christmas".

Emergency accommodation will be provided to end the need for rough sleeping alongside practical support for any health needs, as part of a Â£442m package.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said Burnham promised to end rough sleeping in Greater Manchester when mayor of the area but "failed because he didn't do the hard work necessary".

Burnham's pledge seeks to build on the success of Everyone In, a Covid pandemic-era scheme that saw thousands of rough sleepers housed in hotels and temporary accommodation.

About 37,000 people were helped by that scheme, following its launch in March 2020. The charity Shelter found that about a quarter of them had found settled accommodation, in the form of housing lasting at least six months., external

The PM's announcement comes with an additional Â£102m in new funding, taking Burnham's total commitment to tackling rough sleeping to Â£442m since becoming prime minister.

The money is said to be "fully funded" within the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.

As well as providing immediate support to get people off the streets, the funding is also designed to deliver more than 1,000 homes over the next three years to provide rough sleepers with permanent accommodation.

The funding will also provide "intensive wraparound support", typically psychiatric and drug and alcohol services to help people rebuild their lives.

Burnham said he did not believe "anybody should be forced to sleep rough".

He added: "And actually when you do leave people sleeping rough it can often cost more to the state because people can be in and out of A&E, in and out of hospital beds and sometimes in contact with the police."

The prime minister said the government funding "may not fully get us there" as he appealed to charities and faith organisations to help ensure an offer is made to everybody who needs it.

He added: "We did it in the pandemic. We can do it again."

The government said areas facing the greatest pressures will get the largest share of support.

It added guidance will make clear the need to ensure "adequate and accessible provision" for female rough sleepers, who it says are often underrepresented in official statistics and can be at greater risk of violence, abuse and exploitation.

Rooms in shared flats or houses, B&B accommodation, warm spaces for short-term refuge and supported lodgings are among the types of accommodation mentioned in the guidance that could be used to bring people in off the streets.

News.title: French civil servant drugged us to make us urinate on ourselves, say accusers
News.content:
"I was really weak. I couldn't really feel my legs any more," says AnaÃ¯s de Vos. "I was scared. I didn't know what was happening."

It was July 2011 and AnaÃ¯s, who was then 27, was being interviewed for a job at France's Ministry of Culture in Paris.

She didn't usually drink coffee but when the interviewer, a senior civil servant called Christian NÃ¨gre, offered her one, she agreed out of politeness.

He made it himself, she tells BBC Global Women, but "it tasted badâ¦ so I drank about half".

The meeting had started in the office, but after a few minutes NÃ¨gre suggested they go outside.

As they strolled through Paris's streets, AnaÃ¯s began to feel an inexplicable and uncontrollable need to urinate.

She felt uncomfortable telling NÃ¨gre that she wanted return to the office to use the toilet, so told him she was cold as an excuse to go back to the building. But she says he walked away, guiding them towards the banks of the River Seine, so she told him she needed to find a toilet urgently.

"He looked me right in the eye and said, 'Oh, do you need a wee?'

"I felt like a child. I thought it was really weird the way he looked at me, almost gleeful."

She says he directed her to the door of a storage cupboard under a bridge on the Seine and said: "You can do it here."

Now, AnaÃ¯s is one of nearly 250 women who believe NÃ¨gre drugged them in alleged incidents between 2009 and 2018, subjecting them to what is known as chemical submission, where drugs are used to gain control over someone.

The concept of chemical submission came to prominence in France in 2024 when Gisele Pelicot's husband was found guilty of sedating her and inviting strangers to rape her while she was unconscious.

News.title: Emma Barnett reveals she 'had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have'
News.content:
BBC presenter Emma Barnett has revealed she had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

Barnett, 41, returned to Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday morning, explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

She told listeners: "I made a programme on endometriosis on BBC Two and ended up being in hospital for endometriosis.

"So yes, I've been recuperating, shall we say, from surgery for endometriosis and a hysterectomy to boot. So that's been less fun than the Today programme, but it is lovely to be back."

Barnett's announcement came soon after she published a blog about the "hysterectomy I never wanted to have", external.

The presenter, who has two children, said it was "totally surreal" to be in hospital on the night her documentary was broadcast in June, only well enough to watch the final 10 minutes.

"Some 48 hours before the documentary aired - I had undergone a near-5 hour surgery and somehow found myself lying in bed recovering from extensive endometriosis surgery, a hysterectomy and a gallbladder removal," she wrote.

"Triple threat. Go big or go home. Life imitating art."

She added: "I felt blind-sided and robbed, even though my care had been superb and doctors, utterly brilliant.

"But this was not the road I had envisioned for myself. I had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have."

Endometriosis is where cells similar to those in the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body, resulting in what Barnett has described as "bone-grinding, life-altering pain". It affects one in 10 women and there is no known cure.

A hysterectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the womb (uterus). A hysterectomy alongside removal of endometriosis can reduce the risk of recurrence, according to Endometriosis UK, external.

In her blog, Barnett also said she suspected most of her pain may have been down to another condition, adenomyosis, which can be treated by a hysterectomy.

Her surgery was necessitated after she had an ultrasound while filming the final scene of the documentary, and a problem in her gallbladder was found. "Suddenly things became urgent and non negotiable."

The broadcaster added that she was hopeful that the surgery had helped.

She wrote: "Early indications are that the pain is very much improved - although I am still healing from the surgery itself so that also feels uncertain and frightening to admit - even to myself."

News.title: OpenAI slows down training after its AI carried out hack
News.content:
OpenAI says it has slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.

In a blog post, external, the ChatGPT-maker said it was introducing new measures after its AI agents autonomously bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.

It said training would be slowed for two weeks while it puts the upgrades in place.

"The capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating," the company said. "Our ability to understand...and secure them must stay ahead."

Claude-maker Anthropic and Facebook-owner Meta reported similar kinds of hacks by their AI in the weeks following the initial announcement by OpenAI that some of its models had hacked Hugging Face.

But the firm said it had not stopped AI development altogether. Instead, the pause would be taking place on "reinforcement learning training on our latest models".

This is a training method in which AI models improve through direct feedback, which improves their ability to carry out tasks and respond to users more effectively.

The company it would also expand the systems it uses to monitor dangerous behaviour, and introduce additional safety checks before resuming larger-scale training.

"Model progress is now extremely rapid," OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman posted on X, external about the measures.

"We always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety."

The pause was met with cautious optimism by some in the AI sphere - though others remained sceptical.

Professor Gina Neff, executive director of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, said OpenAI was making "the case for safety by press release" and questioned whether voluntary company safeguards were sufficient without greater government oversight.

"Which is it: OpenAI can be trusted to voluntarily put in place safeguards that actually work, or they are pushing forward with choices to make software that puts society at greater risk," she said.

"Very happy to see this," posted AI analyst Zvi Mowshowitz, external, though he added that "details" and "follow-through" from the initial measures mentioned were also important in order to take a full view on the plans.

News.title: Jury discharged in Palestine Action Elbit raid trial
News.content:
A jury has been discharged in the trial of eight Palestine Action activists who were accused of helping to organise a raid on the UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.

Ian Sanders, Aleksandra Herbich, Teuta Hoxha, Sean Middleborough, Julija Brigadirova, Hannah Davidson, Madeleine Norman and William Plastow were charged with criminal damage after a raid on Elbit Systems in Filton, near Bristol, in August 2024.

They were all also charged with violent disorder, although Plastow was previously found not guilty of this offence.

The group denied any wrongdoing and have been on trial at the Old Bailey since 22 June. Judge Patrick Field discharged the jury earlier after 37 hours of deliberations.

The court heard none of the defendants were at Elbit during raid but were alleged to have helped to plan it, including by compiling an equipment list, reconnaissance, purchasing tools and weapons used by others, and co-ordinating the break-in and its filming.

The Crown Prosecution Service will now need to decide whether to seek a retrial.

A hearing has been set for 14 September to decide the future of the case.

News.title: Scientists 'stunned' by children's lung recovery in ultra low emission zone
News.content:
Scientists say they have been "stunned" by how quickly young children's lungs began to recover and grow after pollution restrictions were brought in where they lived.

Researchers found that children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution showed impressive improvements after the introduction of an Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in 2019 reduced emissions.

The study followed more than 3,400 primary school children in London and Luton and provides what scientists believe is the strongest evidence yet that local clean air zones could help reduce some of the harm caused by pollution during childhood.

But independent researchers caution that other factors must also be considered.

Air pollution can stunt the growth of young children's lungs leaving them at an increased risk of asthma, heart disease, diabetes and even premature death.

Children are also more vulnerable to pollution because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. And when outside, they tend to be closer to the ground and nearer sources of exhaust fumes, for example.

In 2020 Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl from London who died following an asthma attack in 2013, became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed as a cause of death.

In the study, researchers recruited six to nine-year-olds attending primary schools in London's ultra low emission zone and followed the same children for five years, comparing them to similar children (in terms of socio-economic background, physical activity and ethnicity) in Luton.

Children in the study had annual lung function and capacity tests in the year before Ulez came in and for four years after.

Initial results showed children's lungs in London were smaller in capacity than those in Luton, which is less polluted than London but has a similar mix of pollutants.

At the end of the study the children's lung capacity reached near identical levels in both groups.

"While we would expect children's lungs to grow year on year, our results indicate that the London children's lung growth had accelerated during the four years to 'catch up' with the control group in Luton to reach similar levels of lung capacity," researchers say.

"I was absolutely stunned when I first saw the results," Prof Chris Griffiths, a senior author on the study, at Queen Mary University of London, told the BBC.

"The speed of catch up in lung capacity in the London group was surprising and impressive.

"This shows an ambitious clean air zone can drive pollution levels down, rapidly restoring children's stunted lung growth."

The main test measured how much air a child could forcibly breathe out in one second after a big breath in.

In practical terms the improvements could mean children in the London group could run as fast as the Luton group without getting out of breath or blow out the same number of candles for example, Griffiths explained.

Another way of testing for lung capacity used in the study showed significant improvements too, though not to the same extent - implying there are still gains to be made.

Overall the proportion of children in London whose lung capacity was deemed "clinically impaired" (suggesting lung damage resulting in coughs or breathlessness) fell from 14% to 9%.

In Luton - where some smaller scale measures were put in place to tackle air pollution - the figures were 9% to 7%.

The team's measurements also showed the level of nitrogen dioxide children were exposed to fell faster in London than in Luton over this time.

Researchers say this is key as it likely demonstrates that the improved lung growth they saw was related to air quality improvements following the implementation of Ulez.

London's Ulez was first introduced in 2019 by Mayor Sadiq Khan in a bid to "clean up London's air". London had high levels of the harmful gas nitrogen dioxide which comes from motor vehicles.

Older, more polluting vehicles had to pay a daily charge to drive in central London. The measures were later expanded to cover the whole capital. While many supported the policy it provoked political opposition and protests.

News.title: Two jailed for violent disorder at asylum hotel
News.content:
Two men have been jailed for more than two years after taking part in protests outside an asylum hotel in Essex last summer.

An "aggressive mob" of hundreds of people gathered outside the Bell Hotel in Epping, Essex, in July 2025, after one of the migrants living there was charged with sexual assault, Chelmsford Crown Court heard.

Jonathan Glover, 47, from Springfields, Waltham Abbey, was sentenced to two years and six months in prison for violent disorder.

Charlie Land, 24, from Warren Close in Hatfield, Hertfordshire, sobbed as he received a two year and eight month sentence for violent disorder and criminal damage.

The pair were found guilty at Chelmsford Crown Court following a trial in June.

News.title: Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise
News.content:
Competition for degree apprenticeships in England has quadrupled over the past three years, the BBC has found.

The popularity of degree apprenticeships - which offer a paid-for university degree along with a salary - has grown as the cost of university has come under increased scrutiny.

Data seen by the BBC showed the number of applicants through the government's central platform nearly tripled from 8,100 to 21,800 over the past three years, while the number of positions available fell by almost half, from 7,300 to 3,700.

Applicants said they applied to university as a "backup" because competition was so fierce, with employers cutting back on hiring because of high employment costs and economic uncertainty.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it was "backing employers who take on young apprentices".

Last month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure teenagers had technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

His comments came as concerns grow about the immediate and long-term costs of university, with more students wanting to stay at home home rather than moving away, to save money and calls to reform student loan repayments. The cost of undergraduate tuition fees in England is now set to rise every year with inflation.

Degree apprenticeships might look to some like an attractive alternative, but the Freedom of Information data obtained by the BBC suggests they are hard to come by.

News.title: First giant tuna caught off Yorkshire since 1960s
News.content:
Atlantic bluefin tuna have been caught off the coast of Yorkshire for the first time in an estimated 60 years.

The giant fish had not been seen in the North Sea since the 1960s due to overfishing and the depletion of herring shoals, according to researchers from the University of Exeter who have now tagged six off Whitby.

On Sunday, the five-person crew on board The Dominator landed a whopping 338kg specimen before repeating the feat a day later with a fish that weighed "just a little bit" less, according to crew member Jack Gardner.

"I have never caught anything like it," said the 28-year-old from the village of Paull, near Hull, describing it as the "best feeling ever".

Gardner, who has been on board The Dominator since 2018, said the crew had been about 10 miles (16km) from Whitby Harbour on Sunday when they made their first catch.

"It jumped out of the water, we all just looked at each other in awe," he said.

"We couldn't believe that we had actually hooked into one."

News.title: Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School investigated over 'drip pricing'
News.content:
Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and RED Driving School are being investigated by the consumer watchdog over concerns they are not showing full prices upfront to customers.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is examining whether the three companies engaged in so-called 'drip pricing', which is an illegal practice where mandatory fees are not included in the headline price shown to customers.

If the CMA concludes that the firms have broken the law, it can fine them or order them to compensate customers.

The three companies said they were committed to transparency for customers and would engage fully with the CMA.

In the case of Trainline, the CMA said it observed fees of up to Â£2.79 being added on to headline train fares, and up to Â£1.50 for coach bookings.

"Both are costs that can add up for frequent travellers," the CMA said.

Trainline has been accused of drip pricing before. In 2023, the Office of Rail and Road said it and six other third-party train ticket sellers were not being upfront about fees.

Virgin Atlantic is being investigated to see whether mandatory resort fees and local taxes were included in the upfront prices shown to customers buying package holidays. The CMA said these fees vary but can go up to hundreds of pounds, significantly increasing the cost of a holiday.

And the watchdog is looking into whether RED Driving School included mandatory booking fees and digital fees in the upfront price shown to people buying driving lessons. The CMA said the fees could be more than Â£7 per lesson.

Earlier this year, the CMA ordered two other driving schools to give refunds to more than 80,000 customers after they did not disclose the total price for lessons upfront during the online booking process.

Emma Cochrane, the CMA's executive director for consumer protection, said: "The first price customers see should be the price they pay.

"At a time when many households are watching every pound they spend, it is important that people are not surprised by extra fees when booking train and coach tickets, holidays or driving lessons."

A spokesperson for Virgin Atlantic Holidays said it takes its responsibility to customers "incredibly seriously", adding: "we always want to ensure they can make an informed decision when booking a holiday with us.

"Mandatory fees are indicated at multiple stages throughout the booking journey. We are reviewing the points raised by the CMA carefully and will cooperate fully with its investigation."

A Trainline spokesperson said the company was "committed to offering customers a transparent booking experience with clear pricing and genuine value.

"We've proactively engaged with the CMA over several months and we are taking proactive steps to enhance how certain fees are presented to our customers."

Red Driving School said it was disappointed at being included in a wider investigation.

"Red Driver Training always values both transparency and consumer satisfaction in all of our interactions with our customers," a spokesperson said.

"We take any and all of our obligations under consumer law with utmost focus and seriousness."

Since last year, the CMA has had the power to rule that consumer laws have been broken without having to take businesses to court.

Consumer rights group Which? said the CMA should not hesitate to use these powers, "especially after each firm has already received a warning advisory letter".

Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, said: "Following comments made by the Prime Minister last week that unfair pricing practices have no place in our economy, this move sends a clear message to other businesses to follow the rules.

"At a time when household budgets are under strain, consumers must have confidence that businesses aren't there to rip them off and that the regulator is willing to step in to protect their rights."

News.title: Double murder investigation launched over two deaths in Glasgow
News.content:
Police added that officers have trawled hours of public and private CCTV footage as part of the investigation, while door-to-door enquiries are also continuing.

The last sighting of either man had been on Friday morning.

Police also said the Chancellor Street property where the bodies were found was the home of one of the victims, and that the two men knew each other.

Det Supt Kelly said: "I am appealing directly to anyone with any information, no matter how small or insignificant they feel it may be, to come forward and speak to us.

"Please do not assume that the police already know the information you have.

"We are keen to hear from anyone who knew Paul and Gary or who was in the Partick area near to Chancellor Street from Friday morning from 09:00, who saw Paul or Gary, or saw or heard anything suspicious."

Supt Craig Brady said: "I would like to extend my sympathies to the family and friends of Paul and Gary as they try to come to terms with their loss.

"We understand the significant impact this will have on the local community and I would like to thank everyone for their help so far."

Post-mortem examinations took place on Monday and Tuesday and confirmed the causes of death as being murder.

A major incident public portal has been launched, external as part of the investigation.

News.title: Camilla admits it was 'difficult' to keep King's cancer diagnosis a secret
News.content:
Queen Camilla has spoken for the first time about the pressure of keeping King Charles III's cancer diagnosis secret in the early stages of treatment.

In a video to mark the 30th anniversary of Maggie's cancer charity, the Queen, who is president of the charity, recalls how "difficult" it was to avoid discussing her husband's treatment while on an official engagement with cancer patients and their families.

In January 2024, the Queen opened a new Maggie's cancer support centre at the Royal Free Hospital in London.

She had just found out that the King had cancer and would need treatment but had to hold back from telling anyone as the official announcement had not been made public.

"Nobody could say anything at the time, that was quite difficult.

"I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn't the time to say," the Queen told the chief executive of Maggie's, Dame Laura Lee.

"It was just a week before it became public and the courage that must have taken for you," Dame Laura told the Queen - referring to how personally challenging the hospital visit must have been.

"I was just longing to let it out, but obviously I couldn't," the Queen said.

The King's cancer diagnosis was revealed on 5 February 2024, just days after the Queen's engagement at the Royal Free Hospital.

More than two years later, he is still receiving cancer treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated that his health continues to move in a "positive direction".

In the seven-minute film recorded at Clarence House, the Queen says the King's way of coping has always been to push on with official duties. She spoke of helping to look after her "poor husband".

"Nothing stopped him. He just said, 'This is my way. I'm going to cope with it,'" she said.

During the visit, the Queen described feeling aware that she was now sharing the experience of so many families she met.

"I was almost questioning them. I didn't want to pry too deeply. But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don't know, I felt it was much more deep," the Queen said.

"I looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were."

The King has never disclosed the type of cancer he has, but has engaged widely with those treating and supporting cancer patients.

Maggie's says the King's public announcement prompted a 12% increase in men contacting them with a cancer diagnosis.

"The King's openness about his diagnosis has undoubtedly helped others to be more open themselves, and to now hear the Queen's completely understandable and natural response as a wife shines a light on why it is so important that family and friends also get the support they need," said Dame Laura.

"To hear her speak so powerfully of her own emotions when visiting the Royal Free centre, while knowing about his Majesty's diagnosis, is a huge honour."

Maggie's has 27 centres across the UK, built in the grounds of major NHS cancer hospitals, and supports hundreds of thousands of people each year.

News.title: Man convicted after mistaken identity cigarette fine
News.content:
A man has received a criminal conviction for not paying a fine for dropping a cigarette butt, even though he says he has never smoked.

Lucas Harbourd, 49, was fined for littering in Bristol city centre in December 2024, but said he only found out in July when he received a court letter which said he owed Â£458.

He later challenged the fine, with 3GS, the company contracted to hand out fines on behalf of Bristol City Council, admitting it was a case of mistaken identity. But he said he still has to overturn the conviction which he believes could impact his career.

The council and 3GS did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

3GS enforcement officers can issue fines for environmental offences, including littering, graffiti, fly-tipping, leaving dog mess on the street and drinking alcohol where it is banned.

The private company, which has been contracted by the council since 2019, gives out, on average, about 450 fixed penalty notices (FPNs) in the city every month.

A freedom of information request, external revealed that 97% of fines between 2023 and 2025 were for littering.

The Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) previously revealed the vast majority of littering fines involved cigarette butts, which could land a person with a Â£175 fine.

An ADHD charity has called for the public to complain about Channel 4’s latest documentary to Ofcom after its presenter labelled the disorder a “social construct”.

The Great ADHD Myth?, which aired last night (Tuesday 18 August) on Channel 4, sees presenter and NHS psychiatrist Max Pemberton speak to medical professionals who are sceptical about Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) being a legitimate medical condition, particularly in young children.

ADHD is recognised by the NHS as a condition where those affected struggle to concentrate or sit still. Symptoms can include having high energy levels, getting easily distracted, being forgetful, losing things often and finding it hard to organise your time.

However, Pemberton’s documentary questions whether ADHD is a neuro-developmental disorder, how it should be treated and who benefits from the rise in diagnoses over the last few years. It also conducts an experiment which sees 10-year-old Mason stop taking his ADHD medication, which he has taken for two years, over a six-week period to see whether consuming less sugar, banning screen time and introducing yoga helps instead. While initially deciding to keep Mason off his medication, claiming that it had “dulled his sparkle”, she placed him back on it two months later after his performance in school declined.

open image in gallery Mason, 10, takes part in an experiment in the controversial documentary ( Minnow Productions )

Now, charity ADHD UK has responded to the film, revealing that it has complained to Ofcom, and is encouraging others to do the same. “ADHD is not a myth. It is not a social construct. And the programme’s own end credits told you what its sixty minutes wouldn’t: the boy at its centre went back on his medication, and his schoolwork improved,” the organisation said in a statement on Tuesday.

“Their experiment disproved their conclusion. They aired their version anyway. We have already complained to Ofcom. A fuller submission follows, built on the impact data you give us below. We deserve better than this.”

The charity also asked its social media follows to “consider filling in our survey and complaining to Ofcom” over the documentary’s claims – adding that it will also take its findings to Parliament .

Its chief executive, Henry Shelford, called the documentary “sensationalist nonsense” and “one-sided”, revealing that he wrote to Channel 4 to ask for corrections to be made as well as a title change.

“I wish Channel 4 had done what they did for the menopause with Davina McCall, or for dyslexia with Jamie Oliver,” he told The Mirror. “They did shows which were trying to demolish the myths, whereas this show is trying to exacerbate myths. It’s a shame they didn’t do what they are often so good at which is getting a deeper understanding of the reality of an issue using experts who are leaders in their field.

“We wouldn’t have The Menopause Myth or The Dyslexia Myth or The Migraine Myth, so why this? It shows the prejudice and the stigma around ADHD.”

open image in gallery Max Pemberton speaks to medical professionals who are sceptical about ADHD being a condition ( Minnow Productions )

He added that 80 per cent of people find that ADHD medication has a positive impact, and that he was “so angry” by the documentary’s experiment with just one child. “I nearly fell off my chair at the end when the experiment hadn’t worked. It pretends to be science-led but compares a sample size of one to the experience of millions and it obfuscates the truth by spending an hour building a story of a child not needing medication by doing yoga and forest walks and having less screen time and then at the end, through epilogue text, admits that the child struggled in school.”

Others hit out at the documentary online, with broadcaster India Willoughby writing: “Really disappointing that Channel 4 – the channel you’d think most likely to remain sane during the culture war – is showing a programme tonight called The Great ADHD Myth?. Thinking the question mark excuses it. Grim.”

Economic justice campaigner Richard Murphy said that Channel 4 should “hang its head in shame”, pointing out that the documentary lacked interviews with psychologists who believed the condition exists – and anyone else with the disorder other than 10-year-old Mason.

“The most obvious thing to say is that this was a massively arrogant and profoundly unbalanced programme, clearly intended to present a biased view on a subject where the opinion presented will cause significant harm to a very large number of people in the UK,” he wrote in his blog. “That, I think, was unforgivable.”

A Channel 4 spokesperson said in a statement to The Independent: “Channel 4 has a remit to stimulate public debate and challenge the status quo, which includes offering a platform to a range of different views across the broadness of our slate.

“Not everyone will agree with everything included in the programme and we acknowledge the strength of feeling that this subject evokes, however there is considerable public debate in this area and testing conventional thinking and exploring different ideas, as is the case with The ADHD Myth?, is a legitimate part of Channel 4’s remit. Channel 4 has also aired a number of other programmes on the topic of ADHD, which cover a variety of other viewpoints including: Do You Have ADHD?, Johnny Vegas: Art, ADHD & Me and Sam Thompson: Is This ADHD?”

While the documentary provoked backlash, it received positive reviews from some outlets. The Guardian called it the “most controversial show of the year” in which Pemberton “answers his questions convincingly”, while The Times also said that “much of this hour felt convincing, or at least the start of a necessary discussion”.

A defect in a railway track has been discovered where a train derailed last week near Lewes, East Sussex, investigators say – and it had been there before the accident.

Thirty people were injured, two seriously, when the rear three carriages derailed and tipped over onto the embankment.

Police declared a major incident when some passengers were trapped inside the train in scorching temperatures, while others walked along the sides of the overturned train to escape.

open image in gallery A newly released photograph shows the three carriages on their sides ( Rail Accident Investigation Branch )

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB), releasing its preliminary findings, now says rear-facing CCTV photos from trains on the day showed a defect on the line just outside Lewes railway station.

“CCTV images obtained from preceding services using these lines on 13 August show that a track geometry irregularity existed on the immediate approach to the point of derailment, prior to the accident occurring,” it said.

Investigators also say they have received reports from passengers on other trains of “rough riding” at that spot.

About 150 people had been on the train, which was travelling from London Victoria to Eastbourne via Haywards Heath and Lewes on Thursday.

One survivor later described the experience as “completely terrifying”.

“There was a banging. Everything just went topsy-turvy,” said 56-year-old Yana Ludwig, from the United States.

“It seemed like a really long time, but it probably was 10 seconds of that before the carriage actually fell on the side.”

open image in gallery Rail workers and police officers investigate at the scene where a train with around 150 people on board derailed near Lewes ( PA )

Rob Bradley, who was on board with his young daughter, told how his carriage “jumped upwards” as passengers were thrown forwards.

“The train kind of skidded for quite a while before it stopped.

“Only then, when we turned around, did we see the whole back of the train was open and smoke and dust were pouring into the carriage.”

Ambulance crews, air ambulances, critical care paramedics, fire crews and police rushed to the scene.

Of the people hurt, 20 needed hospital treatment, two of them with serious injuries, while “significant damage” was caused to the train and railway infrastructure, RAIB said.

One witness said they saw some people with head injuries and blood down their clothing.

Josh Parker, 22, who was travelling home from work when the train came off the tracks, filmed himself and other passengers climbing out of a sideways carriage and walking on the outside.

The experts say they are analysing data from the black box in the front vehicle, and data from the remaining recorders on the train will also be obtained.

Preliminary analysis shows the driver applied the train’s brakes as it passed the point of derailment, and that the train, which had been going at around 65mph, had started to slow down. The maximum speed on that stretch of line is 70mph.

CCTV recordings, signalling data and radio communications data have also been obtained, the investigators say. The train, track and embankment have been surveyed using various methods including laser scanning and aerial photography.

The accident happened at the height of last week’s heatwave, when temperatures in the southeast reached the high 30s.

RAIB said its investigation would consider the weather, as well as the status of the track, embankment, condition of the train and the effectiveness of any measures taken to address potential issues caused by hot weather.

open image in gallery Investigators have found a rail track defect where a train derailed in East Sussex last week, injuring 30 people (Network Rail/PA) ( Network Rail )

The experts say the land there “is sensitive to variations in water content and may undergo movement as moisture levels change”. They said: “Although, at this stage, there is no evidence to indicate that a significant embankment slip occurred before the accident, there is evidence that some movement had previously taken place.”

Evidence of previous track maintenance activity in the area has been seen.

The railway line will remain closed for at least another week.

Network Rail and Southern Rail said the carriages that fell would need to be carefully lifted away by crane.

They said the location made the removal particularly difficult because the railway is close to a river, in a site of special scientific interest, and restricted road access was via a residential area. The RAIB said its experts would ensure that evidence was preserved while doing this.

Once the train, 1F34, has been removed, engineers will be able to assess the damage to the railway and “understand the scale of the repair work needed before services can resume safely”.

The RAIB has promised to publish its findings, including any recommendations to improve safety, at the end of its investigation.

Halloween trick-or-treating could be less sugary than usual this year as consumers look for healthier snacks and candy companies such as Hershey HSY.N, the United States' biggest chocolate-maker, adapt their product offerings.

Fuelled by GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and a growing focus on health, eating habits are changing, leading the makers of sweet and salty snacks to adjust their portfolios to offer more protein, smaller-sized products and fewer calories.

In the run-up to Halloween on October 31, which can account for nearly a fifth of annual confectionery retail sales, Hershey has added more salty snacks such as popcorn, cheese puffs and pretzels to its trick-or-treat offering, which its research has found U.S. consumers begin stocking up on months in advance.

open image in gallery Halloween trick-or-treating could be less sugary than usual this year ( Getty Images )

"Certainly, the Lesser Evil brand and our salty snacks brands broadly, Skinny Pop and Pirate's Booty, having a greater presence in Halloween is in response to the (healthy eating) dynamic," Dan Mohnshine, Hershey's vice president for demand creation, strategy and innovation, told Reuters.

But he said chocolate was still the Halloween snack of choice.

"When it comes to GLP-1s, we've seen pretty strong resilience in the chocolate category here in the U.S.," he said.

Without giving precise figures, he said early-season sales of snack-size bags of chocolates and sweets had risen in double-digits versus a year ago.

Sugar-free versions, sweetened with sugar alcohols rather than conventional sugar, are also a growth area.

U.S. dollar sales in Hershey's Zero Sugar candy, mint and gum business grew around 4.3 times from 2020 through 2025, Mohnshine said.

AI-driven innovation and the ‘trunk-or-treat’ trend

According to Hershey's "Unwrapping Halloween" report, published in partnership with data intelligence firm Morning Consult this month, three of the five biggest-selling U.S. candies at Halloween are Hershey's products and two-thirds of parents have already bought Halloween treats in the summer.

Further research from the National Confectioners Association found that in 2024, Americans spent $7.4 billion on treats, accounting for 18% of all confectionery retail sales that year.

Given the amount at stake, Hershey is using artificial intelligence to speed up product development.

"We've removed about three months from the typical timeframe it takes to go from consumer insight to approved concept," Mohnshine said. "As a result, our innovation pipeline over the last nine months has expanded 75%."

AI also identifies "trunk-or-treat" parties as a growing trend. They began in COVID lockdowns and are still favoured by communities and families who gather with their cars to exchange treats.

Mohnshine is expecting them to be more popular than ever this year and says the Reese's maker is at the ready with its expanded range of small, individually wrapped pieces that he said are "the key to remaining relevant".

Emergency responders are attending an incident off the Sussex coast following reports of four people in difficulty in the open water.

Several ambulances and two air ambulances were seen near the RNLI station in Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex, on Tuesday afternoon.

A Sussex Police spokesperson said: “Emergency services are currently responding to reports of four people in difficulty in the water close to Shoreham Fort.

“A section of the A259 in Shoreham has been closed as the incident remains ongoing, and we’re urging the public to stay clear of the area in the meantime

“We will provide more information as soon as we are able to.”

The A259 Brighton Road was blocked in both directions from New Road to Kingston Lane because of the incident.

An RNLI spokesman said: “Shoreham RNLI were tasked by HM Coastguard at approximately 3pm on Tuesday 18 August.”

At the scene an ambulance could be seen leaving under a police escort with blue lights flashing.

A HM Coastguard spokesman added: “HM Coastguard responded to an incident reported at Shoreham at about 2.45pm on 18 August.

“An HM Coastguard helicopter was sent as well as Littlehampton, Shoreham and Newhaven Coastguard Rescue Teams, and an RNLI lifeboat from Shoreham.

“Sussex Police and South East Coast Ambulance Service also attended.”

The South East Coast Ambulance Service also said they were responding to reports that four people needed medical attention after getting into difficulty in the water near Shoreham Harbour.

“We were called shortly after 3pm and have a number of ambulance resources at the scene,” a spokeswoman said.

“We have no further information to share at this time but will provide updates as soon as possible.”

If you weren’t sick enough of scrolling through the many social media posts of people’s Ibiza holidays, Good Morning Britain’s Susanna Reid has snuck one in before the end of August.

The Good Morning Britain presenter couldn’t be further away from the ITV show as she was seen partying it up in the Spanish clubbing capital before returning to the morning programme desk.

The broadcaster, 55, has been away from the show throughout the summer, with holiday presenters filling in while the main hosting line-up is away.

However, Reid brought a bit of GMB with her to Wayne Lineker’s beach club O Beach after it was announced that the show had been nominated for Best Daytime Programme at the National Television Awards.

Having left her blouses behind, Reid – seen in a swimming costume and shorts – posed in front of cozzie-donned women holding up a sign which read: “VOTE GMB,” posting it to Instagram.

“We are up for Best Daytime Programme at the incredible @officialntas so I celebrated at one of Ibiza’s best daytime clubs @obeachibiza,” Reid wrote in the caption. “VOTE GMB link in my bio.”

Her co-hosts flocked to the comments, with Rob Rinder posting a series of clapping emojis, while weather presenter Alex Beresford said: “This is how you do it!”

Frequent contributor Ashley James wrote: “Iconic x,” while presenter Paul Brand said: “@GMB never does anything half hearted!”

Lineker, who is the brother of presenter Gary Lineker and owns O Beach Ibiza, added: “Got my vote,” with emojis of the number 100, winky face, raised hands and an orange heart.

Last month, Reid reunited with her former co-presenter Piers Morgan on GMB, five years after his dramatic ITV exit.

Susanna Reid on ‘Good Morning Britain’ ( ITV )

In 2021, Morgan stormed off the show’s set after being criticised by Beresford over his comments about the Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex. Following Markle’s interview with Oprah Winfrey, Morgan said that he “didn’t believe a word” she said about having suicidal thoughts during her time as a senior royal.

Morgan later stepped down as an anchor of GMB and left ITV. He also appeared to backtrack on his initial condemnation of Markle, saying that he may “still have serious concerns about the veracity of a lot of what” she said, but it was “not for me to question if she felt suicidal”.

Reid, who joined GMB in 2014 as a lead presenter, has continued hosting the show ever since alongside the likes of Richard Madeley, Kate Garraway, Ben Shephard and Ed Balls.
