World.title: Warsaw Uprising veteran and activist Wanda Traczyk-Stawska dies aged 99
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Wanda Traczyk-Stawska, a veteran of the Warsaw Uprising against Nazi-German occupation during World War Two, has died aged 99. Traczyk-Stawska, who survived imprisonment in German camps after the uprising, in her later years became a vocal advocate for the rights of women and disabled people. “Warsaw has lost someone extraordinary,” wrote Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, announcing her death on Wednesday. “A heroine, a soldier…but above all a teacher who, throughout her life, taught us what matters most: courage, dignity, and responsibility for our fellow human beings.” Odeszła Pani Wanda. Trudno w to uwierzyć. Warszawa straciła kogoś wyjątkowego – Bohaterkę, żołnierkę Powstania Warszawskiego, Honorową Obywatelkę miasta. Ale przede wszystkim nauczycielkę, która przez całe życie uczyła nas tego, co najważniejsze: odwagi, godności i… pic.twitter.com/uSNcsZ7c1P — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) August 19, 2026 Traczyk-Stawska, born in Warsaw in 1927, was only 12 years old when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. She initially became involved in the Grey Ranks (Szare Szeregi), an underground resistance movement associated with the Polish scouting movement, participating in sabotage operations. She later joined the Home Army (AK), Poland’s main resistance force, and, at the age of 17, served as a riflewoman and liaison during the Warsaw Uprising, taking the nom de guerre “Pączek” (meaning “Bud”). Traczyk-Stawska was seriously injured while fighting in the uprising. After the revolt was defeated, she was taken prisoner and subsequently held in various prisoner-of-war camps in Germany until the end of the war. After returning to Poland, Traczyk-Stawska earned a degree in psychology and began working as a teacher of disabled children in Warsaw. At the same time, she became an active figure in commemorating the uprising and its participants. In her final years, Traczyk-Stawska also became politically active. In 2018, she visited parliament to support a protest by disabled people and their carers, who were seeking more state support. Two years later, at the age of 93, she and another female uprising veteran, Hanna Stadnik, joined the mass Women’s Strike protests that broke out in response to the introduction of a near-total ban on abortion under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. “We women will not relent this time,” she told broadcaster TVN at the time. “In the uprising, we fought for our freedom, because there is no dignity without freedom. If we are currently treated like incubators, we have the right to fight for our dignity…We will fight – unarmed, but to the last woman – not to be treated like objects.” Traczyk-Stawska was also among a group of female Uprising veterans who that year criticised PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński for wearing, during a speech condemning the Women’s Strike protests, a badge featuring the anchor symbol that was used by the Home Army during the war. She was also an advocate for women’s rights more broadly. In 2023, in a speech at the 79th anniversary of the uprising, Traczyk-Stawska noted that, “at the beginning, the generals shouted: ‘Why do we need so many women?'” But, by the time the uprising ended, “we had been given the same rights as boys. And we won’t get rid of these rights. Because everyone, whether a man or a woman, is a citizen of this country and has equality written into the constitution”. Her speech then became overtly political, saying that “this [PiS] government needs to be completely changed, as it doesn’t remember that women have their own position enshrined in the constitution. That we are equal to men.” In both the 2020 and 2025 presidential elections, Traczyk-Stawska expressed support for the candidacy of Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that is PiS’s main opponent. However, in both elections, Trzaskowski lost to PiS-backed candidates. Odeszła Wanda Traczyk-Stawska ps. „Pączek” – Bohaterka, Patriotka, wzór odwagi i niezłomności. Pokazywała, że prawdziwy patriotyzm to budowanie wspólnoty, empatia i otwartość na świat. Cześć Jej pamięci! 🕯️🤍 Najgłębsze wyrazy współczucia dla Bliskich. pic.twitter.com/nY0ijDSBlJ — Monika Sikora ⚡️ (@Moni_Sikora) August 19, 2026 Following news of Traczyk-Stawska’s death, many prominent figures paid tribute to her, in particular from the current KO-led ruling coalition. “Farewell, heroine,” wrote KO leader and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, sharing a photo of himself with Traczyk-Stawska and quoting one of her statements: “Do not stand, do not watch when evil happens, but react immediately, for that is your duty.” While she had fought against German occupation, Traczyk-Stawska later called for reconciliation. In her 2023 speech, she called Germany “our best neighbour” and said that the two countries must now “stand together”, including supporting Ukraine against Russian aggression. Today, Germany’s ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, expressed his “great sadness” at Traczyk-Stawska’s death, calling her an “advocate of dialogue in the process of Polish-German reconciliation and a passionate champion of peace, freedom, and human dignity”. „Nie stój, nie patrz, gdy się zło dzieje, tylko reaguj natychmiast, bo to jest twój obowiązek." – Wanda Traczyk-Stawska Żegnaj, Bohaterko. pic.twitter.com/MhfqlszVcI — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland “99% sure” fugitive opposition politician is in pro-Russian breakaway region of Moldova
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia. Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria. Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights. A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026 Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF. However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”. “I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region. "Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy" Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026 Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval. The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position. “If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week. “Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added. In his remarks today, Tusk said that Romanowski’s likely presence in Transnistria “speaks for itself regarding not only Mr Romanowski but the entire political group that covered up for and benefited from such people, and continues to cover up for them”. PiS politicians have largely avoided commenting, noting that it has not been confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. However, deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek last week admitted that, if Romanowski did trael there, he would have “crossed a line”. Nie wyprzedzajmy faktów – powiedział poseł PiS Zbigniew Kuźmiuk, pytany, czy Marcin Romanowski może zostać zawieszony w partii.https://t.co/IQzuS8Ad7O — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 14, 2026 Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government from 2019 until 2023, when the party lost power to a new ruling coalition led by Tusk. In 2024, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 11 crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group and using crime as a source of income. However, he instead fled to Hungary, where he was granted asylum by the then-government of Viktor Orbán, a PiS ally. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, his successor, Péter Magyar, promised to extradite both Romanowski and Zbigniew Ziobro, the former PiS justice minister who had also fled criminal charges in Poland and been granted asylum by Orbán. However, as Magyar was sworn in as the new prime minister, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains, and Romanowski disappeared, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians deny the accusations against them and claim to be victims of political persecution by Tusk’s government. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. He denies wrongdoing and calls the case political revengehttps://t.co/BXdQgWm61q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In his comments on Tuesday morning, Nowak said that prosecutors had found “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. Polish prosecutors are still, however, attempting to confirm Romanowski’s whereabouts and secure his extradition to Poland to face justice. He is subject to a European Arrest Warrant. However, that applies only in EU countries, and Moldova is not a member of the bloc. World.title: FedEx-led €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost wins EU approval
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty). InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February. If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each. Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO — WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026 The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle. The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%. The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing. In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994. InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office. In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence. In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself. However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty. World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) without paying capital gains tax. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build long-term savings and channel billions of zloty into the domestic financial market. Osobiste Konta Inwestycyjne to nowe narzędzie, które ułatwi inwestowanie i oszczędzanie na preferencyjnych warunkach podatkowych. Nowe przepisy wejdą w życie 1 stycznia 2027 r. Szczegóły w komunikacie ⤵️ https://t.co/Z6zEHKkQsY — Ministerstwo Finansów (@MF_GOV_PL) August 13, 2026 The new legislation, which was signed into law on Thursday by President Karol Nawrocki and will take effect on 1 January 2027, creates Personal Investment Accounts (OKI). All assets held in an OKI will be completely exempt from the usual 19% capital gains tax. Amounts up to 100,000 zloty, including up to 25,000 in savings assets such as bonds and deposits, will be completely tax free. Assets above 100,000 zloty will be subject to a new tax on their value. The government has said the tax will amount to 0.85% in 2027 and will be adjusted annually. Finance minister Andrzej Domański earlier described the introduction of OKI as “the biggest change in years for individual investors and the largest project aimed at building domestic capital to drive the development of the Polish economy”. While Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, regularly clashes with the government and has vetoed a record number of laws, in this case he approved their idea, which he office said “could have a positive impact on both citizens and the state”. “Poles will gain a tool to promote family wealth building thanks to an attractive tax-free allowance and a guarantee of no account maintenance fees,” they added. Sejm przyjął ustawę o Osobistych Kontach Inwestycyjnych. Do 100 tys. zł bez podatku. To największa od lat zmiana dla indywidualnych inwestorów i największy projekt budowy krajowego kapitału napędzającego rozwój polskiej gospodarki. 🇵🇱 — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) July 3, 2026 The government estimates the scheme could result in about 74 billion zloty flowing to the Warsaw Stock Exchange by 2040. Kamil Gemra, an assistant professor at the Warsaw School of Economics, said he considered the projection realistic. “Society is getting wealthier; we have record amounts in our bank accounts. It would be enough for just a few per cent of that money to flow into the capital market for the figure cited by the finance ministry be achieved,” Gemra told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The government also forecasts, however, that the tax exemption will reduce state budget revenues by nearly 9 billion zloty over 10 years, at a time when public finances are under increasing strain amid rapidly rising debt. Poland’s WIG20 stock market index has hit its highest ever level, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year, gaining almost 25% https://t.co/CBbv99v2Uk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Poland already has three mechanisms that allow people to accumulate assets with tax advantages: Individual Retirement Accounts (IKE), Individual Pension Schemes (IKZE), and Employee Capital Plans (PPK). However, in all three cases, the capital gains tax exemption is conditional on withdrawing funds after reaching retirement age. Despite the Polish stock market’s strong performance in recent years, Poles’ direct participation remains modest. Shares make up only 2.9% of household assets, the equivalent of 3% of GDP. That is well below the EU average of 8.2%. By contrast, households’ cash holdings are equivalent to 11.5% of GDP, well ahead of the EU average of 4.5% and behind only Slovenia (11.7%) and Germany (11.6%). World.title: Prague’s Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
World.content:
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.

Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.

According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.



The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.

From Barcelona to Prague

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.

Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.

After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.

The First Edition

Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.

Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.

Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.

Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.

Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.

World.title: Czech Fish Farmers Take Emergency Measures Amid Prolonged Drought
World.content:
Fish farmers reduce or suspend supplementary feeding to lower oxygen consumption, reports say.

Fish farmers in the Czech Republic have begun taking emergency measures as a prolonged drought, worsened by high temperatures across Europe, strains water supplies.

Facing water shortages, fish farmers have reduced or suspended supplementary feeding to lower fish oxygen consumption, while ponds are being regularly aerated, according to the report.



Several ponds have also been netted earlier than usual.

In the Třeboň area, which delivers tons of carp for the Czech Christmas table, part of the 200-hectare Koclířov pond has been drained and the fish moved to holding tanks.

More than a third of the water is missing from the region’s famous system of fish ponds due to the drought. The water level in Lake Svět, for example, has fallen by 98 centimetres. High temperatures are also causing water to evaporate more quickly.

The Czech government is expected to address the 2027 budget, upcoming elections and measures to tackle worsening drought.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pledged an extra CZK 4 billion for drought-related measures. If approved, ministers will present plans for implementing them.

World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



You can get your ticket here.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: How Much Can a Prague Taxi Driver Really Earn Each Month
World.content:
For passengers, a taxi ride can make the job look straightforward. Pick someone up, drive them across Prague, wait for the next booking and repeat.

But the income of a full-time taxi driver depends on far more than the fare shown on the meter or app.

Drivers working through platforms such as Uber and Bolt can generate more than CZK 60,000 in gross monthly revenue when working around 40 to 50 hours a week. What they actually keep, however, is considerably less.



Gross income can exceed CZK 60,000

Official figures for Prague’s taxi sector put the average gross monthly pay at roughly CZK 38,000. Drivers who work full time through ride-hailing platforms can earn more, particularly when they concentrate on periods of high demand.

According to Ondřej Krátký, founder of the Czech taxi platform Liftago, drivers can typically earn about CZK 250 to CZK 350 per hour. At the lower end of the market, however, some drivers make only around CZK 80 an hour, which is difficult to turn into a sustainable income in Prague.

Official statistics may also underestimate the money generated by some drivers because not every journey is paid through an app. Cash payments remain part of the business.

Fuel and commissions take a large share

Most Prague taxi drivers operate as self-employed contractors and use their own cars. That means they are responsible for almost all of the costs associated with the job.

Fuel is one of the largest expenses. Someone driving every day can spend more than CZK 10,000 a month on petrol or diesel alone.

Ride-hailing platforms also take a percentage of each fare. Depending on the service and other conditions, commissions can account for roughly 20 to 25 percent of the fare. Drivers must also cover vehicle maintenance, repairs, commercial insurance and the mandatory social and health insurance payments required of self-employed workers.

Once these expenses are taken into account, the amount left from gross earnings can fall by a third or more.

For a full-time driver, a realistic monthly amount after operating costs can therefore be somewhere between CZK 22,000 and CZK 35,000. The exact figure depends on the car, fuel consumption, working hours, platform commissions and the number and type of trips completed.

Tips make only a small difference

Tips are unlikely to transform a taxi driver’s income in the Czech Republic.

Unlike in countries where tipping is a major part of service workers’ earnings, Czech passengers generally round up the fare or leave a relatively small amount.

Uber allows passengers to tip through its app for up to 30 days after a journey, with the full tip going to the driver. Bolt offers a similar feature.

For most drivers, however, tips remain a minor addition to their monthly income rather than a significant source of earnings.

Timing can make a bigger difference

Drivers can increase their income by choosing when and where they work.

Friday and Saturday nights are among the busiest periods in Prague, particularly in the city centre. When demand rises sharply, ride-hailing platforms can increase fares, allowing drivers to generate more revenue from the same number of working hours.

Major concerts, festivals and other large events can have a similar effect. Airport journeys can also be attractive because they tend to cover longer distances than short trips within the city.

World.title: How the busiest Budapest metro line cannot be extended far enough because of the Russians
World.content:
Despite having featured in plans for decades, the proposed Budapest metro line M3 extension to Káposztásmegyer is unlikely to go ahead for many years, based on the current situation. The main obstacle is no longer a lack of money or political will: both the trains operating on the line and the control system supplied by a Russian manufacturer impose serious limits on any expansion.

Even short extension of the busiest Budapest metro line is fraught with difficulties

The investment currently being prepared would extend the line by just two stations. A 1.9-kilometre section would be built from the end of Árpád út, with new stops at Rózsa utca and Rákospalota-Újpest railway station. The project would also include an intermodal transport hub and a 240-space park-and-ride car park.

Even this short section would be difficult to deliver, as several properties would have to be acquired, including social housing, a family home and commercial premises caught up in probate proceedings. In 2021, the cost of compulsory purchases was estimated at 2.8 billion forints. But after property prices rose by 75 to 90 per cent, the bill could now exceed 5 billion forints. To make matters worse, the deadlines for accounting for EU funding fall at the end of 2029 and the end of 2030, leaving very little time because of the sanctions imposed on previous governments, Népszava wrote.

Five stations are needed – but the Russians make that impossible

The full, originally planned five-station extension to Káposztásmegyer faces an even more serious problem. According to a 2025 estimate, the entire investment would cost 158 billion forints. Much of the relevant documentation has since expired, meaning that parts of the planning and approval processes would have to be started again.

The biggest difficulty, however, is the project’s dependence on the Russian company Metrowagonmash. The refurbishment of Line 3 was commissioned from the Russian manufacturer under government pressure. The old Soviet carriages were modernised, but air conditioning was not installed – nor was a modern communications-based train control system, known as CBTC. Instead, the decision was taken to refurbish the existing Russian AVR system.

The current plans are likewise based on extending that system. Yet because the necessary software licences are involved, only a very limited section of the market would be able to carry out the work – in practice, the Russian manufacturer itself.

If you missed- 20 August festivities: crucial public transport changes announced

This creates a particularly awkward situation. BKV has been locked in a legal dispute with Metrowagonmash for years, while the company also appears on the EU sanctions list as a Russian enterprise involved in the war against Ukraine. Although the Hungarian government exempted the maintenance of Budapest Metro Line 3 from the restrictions, the dependence on the Russian company remains.

The existing trains could still serve the two new stations. But the current fleet would be insufficient for the five-station extension to Káposztásmegyer. Without new trains, therefore, the full extension cannot be built, and BKK is planning on the basis that the existing metro carriages will remain in service for the next 20 years.

The Káposztásmegyer connection remains an almost unfathomably distant prospect – much like air-conditioned trains. István Tarlós, the Fidesz-backed mayor of Budapest at the time, said that air conditioning was unnecessary underground. Time and climate change have since proved him wrong: he made the wrong decision by failing to press Budapest’s case on the issue against the Orbán government.

World.title: Sziget Festival 2026 in numbers: foreigners vs Hungarians, unsatisfied organisers, the festival’s future
World.content:
The tourism and economic significance of the Sziget Festival extends beyond the money spent at the festival site: 90 per cent of foreign visitors travelled to Hungary specifically because of the event, leaving HUF 15 billion in the Hungarian economy, GKI Economic Research Co. said on Wednesday, presenting the findings of an on-site survey conducted at the festival to the Hungarian News Agency.

Sziget Festival: foreign festival-goers spend more, remain longer

GKI noted that its questionnaire-based survey, conducted among a sample of 529 people, was not representative, but was nevertheless suitable for assessing the general financial circumstances of visitors.

According to the GKI survey, a foreign festival-goer spent an average of approximately HUF 260,000 in Hungary in connection with Sziget, excluding international travel costs. This figure includes spending both at and outside the festival site, ranging from the festival ticket to accommodation and food and drink in Budapest.

By international standards, Sziget is considered to offer good value for money: only 28 per cent of foreign visitors regarded it as expensive. The survey found that Hungarian visitors spent an average of HUF 108,000.

According to a statement from Sziget, approximately 357,000 people attended this year’s event, based on the cumulative number of daily admissions. Foreign visitors accounted for 47 per cent of the total, while almost half of festival-goers were attending Sziget for the first time. Respondents spent an average of 3.2 days at the festival: 44 per cent stayed for five days, while 31 per cent attended for just one day. Foreign visitors spent an average of 3.5 days at the festival.

Economic impact of Sziget significant

The analysis found that Sziget’s economic impact was not confined to the duration or site of the festival. A significant proportion of festival-goers from outside Budapest, including foreign visitors, spent additional time in the capital and its surrounding area alongside attending the event, generating considerable additional value for the tourism economy.

Festival-goers from outside Budapest, including foreign visitors, spent HUF 98,000 outside Sziget. Of this, 38 per cent went on accommodation, 31 per cent on food and drink, 17 per cent on entertainment and 13 per cent on travel within Hungary.

According to Sziget’s own figures, approximately 58,000 foreign visitors attended the festival this year. Multiplying that figure by the average amount spent per person in Hungary, the festival’s international audience left roughly HUF 15 billion in the Hungarian economy. This was money that would not have entered the country without the festival, since 90 per cent of foreign visitors had travelled there specifically because of Sziget, MTI wrote.

Do you have an interesting story you would like to share with other readers? Write for us!

Organisers not satisfied

The revenue was distributed among accommodation providers, the hospitality sector, transport and other services, and its effects continued to be felt beyond the festival itself. In other words, Sziget’s economic significance is considerably greater than the sums spent at the festival site alone would suggest, GKI said.

“Based on feedback from the audience and the media, the direction we have outlined is good, but many circumstances were not in our favour, so the numbers did not turn out as we would have liked,” Károly Gerendai, the founder of Sziget Festival told media after the event. Last year’s six-day festival attracted 416,000 visitors, he added.

Shock as young man joins women taken ill en masse at Budapest concert and recounts his ordeal

“Last autumn, we suddenly had to take over the festival from the departing foreign owners, and then political disputes almost brought Sziget to an end. In the spring, we were optimistic, but we will fall short of the hoped-for numbers,” Gerendai said.

Károly Gerendai. Photo: MTI

“The organisation and ticket sales started with a four-month delay, whereas previously we had sold a third of our tickets during this early period. The strengthening of the forint made the festival more expensive for foreigners, and the third factor was that among Hungarian ticket buyers, the extreme heatwave, drought, and questions about the power supply created a kind of disaster mentality, which dampened the mood for festival-going,” he concluded.

Gerendai added that there would be Sziget Festival in 2027, the event will be organised between 10 August and 15 August.

World.title: Could Hungarians directly elect a much stronger president next year? This is what one of Tisza’s strongmen now says
World.content:
The possibility of directly electing the president resurfaces from time to time. For now, András Baka was elected by Tisza’s parliamentary majority, but Péter Magyar, the prime minister, has repeatedly indicated that he would support a direct election. Baka, meanwhile, is only an interim president, appointed for the transitional period. One of Tisza’s leading figures, Péter Magyar’s brother-in-law, has spoken about the powers a directly elected president should have and the constitutional changes such a decision would entail.

A directly elected president would be more powerful than the prime minister

Márton Melléthei-Barna previously made headlines after it emerged that Péter Magyar intended to appoint him justice minister. However, Melléthei-Barna eventually withdrew because of their family connection, and Márta Görög became Magyar’s minister instead. Melléthei had previously served as Tisza’s head of legal affairs and supported the campaign throughout. During that period, he met Péter Magyar’s sister, whom he later married.

Melléthei-Barna recently gave an interview to Magyar Hang, which was reported on by Telex. In it, he said that Hungary’s president could be directly elected in the future, although this would raise a number of questions. In his view, the earliest this could happen would be at the end of 2027, because the new constitution could be adopted in the autumn, following a thorough process of public consultation – something Tisza had previously promised. Moreover, the election could not be held until at least 90 days after the adoption of the new constitution.

Gábor Pósfai (l), Péter Magyar (c) and Márton Melléthei-Barna. Magyar announced Melléthei-Barna’s nomination. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

At the same time, he argued that a directly elected president would have a stronger mandate than the prime minister, meaning that the current, limited powers of the presidency would not be sufficient. The powers of the head of state would therefore have to be reconsidered.

He stressed, however, that neither the method of electing the president nor the timing of the adoption of the new constitution had been set in stone.

Would the new directly elected president have greater powers?

One of the key questions surrounding direct presidential elections is precisely what powers the head of state would receive. According to Melléthei-Barna, holding a direct election would not necessarily be justified if the president’s powers remained unchanged.

András Baka was elected by the Parliament on 11 August. Photo: Facebook/Tisza Párt

His argument is that a directly elected head of state would have greater democratic legitimacy than the prime minister while continuing to possess only the current, limited presidential powers. In his view, that would create an unusual constitutional situation, which is why the president’s powers would also need to be reconsidered.

Do you have an interesting story you would like to share with other readers? Write for us!

Melléthei-Barna did not specify exactly what additional powers he considered necessary, or in what direction the role of the head of state should change. The MP said for the time being that he could put forward arguments in favour of a direct presidential election, but that much would depend on the role assigned to the president under the new system.

Sexual abuse, starvation, squalor and accident hazards: Orbán’s government concealed the reality of Hungary’s children’s homes

The prime minister also indicated during a Reddit AMA (Ask Me Anything) discussion in mid-July that he supported direct presidential elections, although he did not explain what this would mean in practice.

Sándor Palace, the home and office of the Hungarian President in the Buda Castle. Photo: Facebook/Dr. Sulyok Tamás

Permanent campaigning?

Analyses published previously suggested that Tisza was preparing for a period of permanent campaigning in the years ahead. This could include the adoption of a new constitution, the election of the president and an early local-government election.

Péter Magyar has repeatedly denied that he is planning an early local-government election, but he has called on compromised mayors to resign.

Tisza’s parliamentary majority elected András Baka president on 11 August, after Tamás Sulyok’s presidential mandate was terminated through a constitutional amendment. Baka took office today.

World.title: Hungary has a new President from today
World.content:
Parliament elected András Baka, the former President of the Supreme Court, as President of the Republic on August 11, after he had been nominated by the governing Tisza group. Baka was elected by MPs in a secret ballot with 140 votes in favour and 6 against, with opposition Fidesz and the Christian Democrats (KDNP) not taking part in the vote.

From today on Hungary’s President is András Baka

In line with the parliamentary resolution on the election, the new head of state is taking office on August 19, and in accordance with the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, his term of office will last until the new constitution comes into force, but for no longer than five years, MTI wrote.

Parliament elected a new President of the Republic because, following the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, Taműs Sulyok’s term as head of state expired at midnight on 20 July. His powers were temporarily assumed by Parliamenary Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer.

Ágnes Forsthoffer and Tamás Sulyok. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes

Previous President did not resign

Péter Magyar, chairman of the Tisza Party, called on President Sulyok — and several other senior state officials appointed by the former Orbán government — to step down from their posts on the night of the April 12 election, which saw the two-thirds victory for the Tisza Party and the defeat of the Fidesz-KDNP coalition that had been in power since 2010.

He repeated this call on several occasions, setting a deadline of May 31 for his resignation, and indicated that if he did not resign, Sulyok would be removed from office by virtue of the powers granted to them. The head of state did not comply with the demand.

Magyar and Sulyok after the 12 April elections: the faces tell us much. Photo: Péter Magyar/Facebook

On 1 June, Magyar, accompanied by the Minister of Justice, visited the President of the Republic and subsequently announced that if Sulyok did not resign from his post, the Fundamental Law would be amended to remove him from office.

On 4 July, the government submitted a proposal to initiate the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, which stated that: on the day following the amendment’s entry into force, the term of office of the incumbent President of the Republic shall cease, and parliament will elect a President of the Republic to serve until the new Constitution comes into force, but for a maximum of five years.

Demonstration for Sulyok held before

Fidesz and KDNP protested against the planned constitutional amendment and, on 9 July, organised a demonstration at the President’s office at Sándor Palace against the “establishment of an authoritarian regime” and the removal of the head of state.

Former President János Áder delivers a speech opposing the proposed amendment to the Fundamental Law at a demonstration organized jointly by Fidesz and the KDNP in front of the Sándor Palace on 9 July, 2026. Photo MTI/Tibor Illyés

On 13 July, parliament adopted the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, and five days later, Sulyok announced that he would sign it, while expressing serious objections to its content, describing the amendment as a grave and shameful historical example of the abuse of political power.

Hungary’s new president Baka already more popular than predecessor Sulyok ever was, poll finds

Sulyok’s removal was not unconstitutional

On 8 August, the Tisza parliamentary group nominated Baka as a candidate for the presidency. The opposition Our Homeland party proposed Máté Tóth, an energy lawyer, for the post, but the six-member parliamentary group failed to attach the signatures of 40 MPs, required for the nomination to be valid.

The Fidesz and KDNP parliamentary groups did not take part in the election of the new President of the Republic, stating that they consider the removal of Sulyok to be illegitimate. The two opposition parties also appealed to the Constitutional Court regarding the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, but on August 17 the Court rejected the petition on the grounds that it lacked jurisdiction.

PM Magyar wished President András Baka good health, “as much humanity as possible” in his work in a Facebook post, MTI wrote.

Photo: MTI

World.title: Sexual abuse, starvation, squalor and accident hazards: Orbán’s government concealed the reality of Hungary’s children’s homes
World.content:
Around 7,000 children currently live in children’s homes in Hungary. A report produced in early 2024 exposed appalling conditions in these institutions, but the Orbán government chose instead to conceal the reality: abuse, a lack of psychological support, starvation, and outdated, unusable furniture and equipment. The new government has promised action, but for now it has only reached the stage of assessing the conditions.

The Orbán government tried to conceal the truth

Starving children, mouldy bathrooms, dangerous furniture and flooring, a shortage of psychologists, and sexual abuse among peers: these were among the findings revealed by child-protection inspection reports commissioned by the Orbán government in early 2024, following the presidential pardon scandal. The government kept the results secret until the very end. Direkt36 eventually obtained the documents through litigation, and following the change of government they were handed over by the successor to the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs, on 31 July.

Former PM Orbán: they found money for everything, but children’s homes did not get anything. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

According to Telex, the government was initially seeking to establish whether sexual abuse had been covered up in other institutions, as it had been in the Bicske case. The inspections found only one such instance. However, the examination of all 530 residential childcare institutions uncovered a large number of other deeply troubling failings.

Abuse, starvation and peer violence

One of the most important lessons from the documents is that the problems extended far beyond individual cases of abuse. A report from Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County found that it was almost commonplace in state-run institutions for children affected by abuse not to receive appropriate psychological support, while a shortage of psychologists had persisted for years. There was also a significant shortage of professionals in other areas: there were too few educators and child supervisors, while staff turnover was another serious problem.

The findings on violence between peers paint an especially grave picture. In Vas County, for example, the number of cases of sexual abuse between children in children’s homes was rising, and the youngest perpetrator was just nine years old. In Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg County, inspectors found that an abuse case at a church-run institution had not been properly investigated.

Abuse in the Szőlő street juvenile detention centre on the footage of a surveillance camera. Photo: PrtScr/Youtube

Perhaps the most shocking case emerged in Bács-Kiskun County. At a specialist children’s home, dinner ended at half past six in the evening, after which the children had no access to bread, butter, jam or any other food. This was despite the fact that the institution housed children who took part in sport and had special care needs; according to the report, they therefore required more food. Citing a police investigation, the document states that some children submitted to sexual abuse by their peers in exchange for food.

Why did the government fail to provide basic conditions?

The physical conditions also fell short of what could reasonably be expected in many institutions. In a Bács-Kiskun County children’s home, inspectors found outdated and dangerous beds and wardrobes, torn furniture and cracked flooring. In Budapest, one building had just two working lights out of 20; elsewhere, donated equipment could not be used because of the outdated electrical wiring. The capital also had bathrooms that were nearly 50 years old and impossible to clean, while several institutions did not even have cleaning staff.

Do you have an interesting story you would like to share with other readers? Write for us!

The building of the Szőlő street juvenile detention centre in Budapest. Following the scandal, the Orbán government decided to close the institution and sold the building as if nothing had happened. Photo: Facebook/Péter Juhász

In Vas County, inspectors also found children’s homes where the bathrooms had become unusable because of leaks. As a result, 12 children had to share a single bathroom, whose walls had become mouldy from the damp and whose plaster was crumbling. According to the report, conditions had deteriorated further since the previous inspection.

Scandal, if true: PM Orbán’s former deputy and opposition KDNP party head Zsolt Semjén accused of raping a minor by victim

Illustration. The Hungarian children’s homes need urgent financial and political aid. Photo: depositphotos.com

The current Ministry of Social and Family Affairs says that, by 2026, the child-protection system had effectively become completely gridlocked, creating an urgent need for new places and a solution to the provision of crisis care. The ministry says it will publish, on 31 August, a report concluding the first part of its Child-Protection Diagnosis, which will also include relevant data from the latest partial report on child protection. Only then might measures finally be introduced to improve conditions.

World.title: Popular Hungarian dairy and food brand Cserpes has a new owner
World.content:
Family-owned cheese maker Profood Flexum has acquired local peer Cserpes Sajtműhely Élelmiszeripari Ltd, the company’s brand consultant told MTI.

No details discolosed about Cserpes transaction

The sides did not disclose the details of the transaction which includes Cserpes‘s entire vertically integrated business. No changes will be made to the brand, its products, its network of shops or its staff.

“The goal is to preserve, further develop and strengthen a successful Hungarian brand,” the statement said. Founder István Cserpes will continue to advise on the brand and play an active role in its future development, MTI wrote.

Profood Flexum operates its own farm and dairy. It counts SAGA, Gallicoop, Spar, Merian Foods, CBA and the pizzeria Don Pepe among its business partners.

A 30+ yo brand

Cserpes Sajtműhely was founded by István Cserpes in 1992. Its products include milk, yoghurt, cheese and Cserpes Trudi. The first Cserpes Tejivó opened in 2012, and the company currently operates three milk bars in Budapest.

Since 2013, the Cserpes brand has received MagyarBrands recognition and has been entitled to display the Superbrands trademark. In 2025, István Cserpes received the Entrepreneur of the Year award from the National Association of Entrepreneurs and Employers.

Last year, Cserpes recorded revenue of HUF 5.073 billion and a post-tax profit of HUF 367 million. In 2024, its revenue stood at HUF 4.5 billion and its profit at HUF 652 million. The company employs approximately 200 people.

World.title: Were foreign students in Hungary Orbán’s next target? Influencer suffers a spectacular backlash
World.content:
A group of “headscarf-wearing women and black men” got off a Hungarian-registered bus at a rest stop near the country’s western border. That was all it took for Virág Gulyás, a journalist and influencer for Mandiner, one of the Orbán regime’s flagship media outlets, to suggest that Péter Magyar had begun the mass resettlement of illegal migrants. It apparently did not occur to her that they might be foreign students.

Fidesz influencer’s narrative fits neatly into Orbán’s propaganda

“There isn’t much of a tourism branding angle on that bus,” Gulyás wrote, swiftly concluding that the passengers could not be tourists and must instead be illegal migrants.

These, of course, are the people against whom the Orbán government claims to have taken action, building a border fence and spending roughly a decade frightening the public with warnings that, unless Fidesz remained in power, the country would be overrun by immigrants.

That narrative only partly reflected reality. The migrants who gathered at Budapest’s Keleti railway station and along the motorways in 2015 were not trying to enter Hungary; they wanted to travel west. Their bottleneck was caused precisely by the closure of Hungary’s western borders.

Since the change of government, it has emerged that the Orbán administration had planned to build a refugee camp in Vitnyéd. It had also long been known that the government had admitted large numbers of guest workers, who have since become indispensable in certain sectors as Hungarian workers have emigrated.

Meanwhile, Péter Magyar has been repeatedly attacked for allegedly welcoming illegal migrants. The Tisza government, however, has consistently made its position clear: it would reject the admission and subsidisation of migrants, maintain the fence along Hungary’s southern border, and co-operate with the European Union in addressing a problem that affects several countries.

Fidesz-linked influencer immediately mistook foreign students for illegal immigrants

Ms Gulyás’s post fitted the Fidesz propaganda machine perfectly. She claimed that a Hungarian-registered bus was carrying “headscarf-wearing women and black men” near Sopron, as though an organised programme of mass settlement had already begun.

Are Orbán’s next target foreign students learning in Hungary? Photo: Facebook/Gulyás Virág kimondja

The National Conference of Student Unions (HÖOK) responded, however, and clarified that the passengers were students enrolled in the Stipendium Hungaricum programme, launched by the Orbán government in 2013.

Do you have an interesting story you would like to share with other readers? Write for us!

They were in Hungary to study and, on returning home, to use the knowledge they had acquired for the benefit of their own countries. They were also expected to remember the generosity of the Hungarian state, which provides scholarships and other forms of support, form lifelong friendships and professional relationships, and thereby help advance Hungary’s national and foreign-policy objectives while improving the country’s image abroad.

Leaked: Fidesz could be dismantled within weeks as its fate rests with members – and János Lázár

HÖOK said that more than 11,000 students were studying in Hungary under the programme this year. The students pictured had been visiting Sopron, where they learned about a wide range of subjects, from the city’s Roman remains and its famous referendum to its rich student traditions, the origins of the Hungarian people and the foundation of the Hungarian state.

Let us hope they took plenty away from the trip — and that the Fidesz influencer’s insulting post did not reach them.

Lots of foreign students acquire their degree in Hungary. Illustration. Photo: Facebook/BME

Rather than apologise, however, Ms Gulyás insulted HÖOK over its response and angrily declared that, although the organisation had now offered an explanation, she would continue photographing every suspicious-looking bus and bringing the matter to public attention.

She even appealed to her 182,000 followers, asking them to send her more pictures of a similar nature.

World.title: New chapter may begin in history of public service media on 20 August
World.content:
The launch of an independent and authoritative news programme on the M1 channel will mark a new chapter in the history of public service broadcasting on the 20 August national holiday, the press and marketing department of Duna Media Services Nonprofit told MTI on Tuesday.

New chapter may begin in history of public service media

An all-day celebratory programme will be hosted by renowned presenters Antónia Mészáros and Ádám Bősze, whose return — limited to this day only — will demonstrate that public media is striving not only to provide credible, accessible and multifaceted information, but also to regain professional autonomy and viewers’ trust, the statement said.

Mészáros is an experienced journalist who had worked for years in the BBC’s most prestigious London newsrooms, and she became known in Hungary’s public media as a resolute reporter who was removed following an interview with then Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in 2010. She later continued her career at commercial news channel ATV, before leaving the screen in 2017 to become executive director of UNICEF Hungary, a position she has held ever since.

Bősze is a leading figure in the promotion of Hungarian culture and music. The music historian worked at Bartók Rádió for over a decade and a half, and he has been a commentator on prestigious opera and concert broadcasts, as well as a television presenter.

Leaked: Fidesz could be dismantled within weeks as its fate rests with members – and János Lázár

Flag-raising, flower carnival, Holy Right Hand, show

The all-day programme on 20 August will feature prominent figures from Hungarian public, cultural and academic life, and public service media crews will be present at all major celebratory events, as well as at gatherings of the Hungarian community in rural areas and abroad.

In keeping with tradition, public service media will broadcast live the flag-raising ceremony, the military parade and the subsequent air show live in Budapest, as well as the Debrecen Flower Carnival, and, in the early evening, the Procession of the Holy Right Hand. From 9.00 PM, viewers will be able to watch live the spectacular show in front of the parliamentary section of the River Danube. As part of the festive programme schedule, the news programme Híradó will again be presented on M1.
