At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: Sacked Ukraine defence minister calls for wartime election
World.content:
Ukraine's ousted Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a wartime election, arguing Ukraine faces a "crisis of governance".

It is the first demand of its kind and would be the first leadership challenge to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Under Ukrainian law, holding elections during wartime is prohibited.

But in Mr Fedorov's video address he said "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia".

"We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war," he said.

Zelenskyy just scored an 'own goal' The Ukrainian president's decision to fire his popular, tech-savvy 35-year-old Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week baffled many. Analysts say what happens next could be pivotal to the war.

The 35-year-old was a longtime ally of Mr Zelenskyy's until his unexpected firing from the Defence Ministry in July, just six months after he was appointed.

He was the last remaining member of Mr Zelenskyy's first cabinet in 2019.

Unlike his predecessors, Mr Fedorov publicly laid out a strategy to defeat Russia through attrition and technological superiority.

Shortly after his dismissal, a bitter rift was exposed between Mr Fedorov and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Protests have been held in Kyiv against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's decision to replace Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

Thousands of Ukrainians then took to the streets demanding the sacking of Mr Syrskyi, who Mr Zelenskyy later dismissed bowing to public pressure.

Protests in support of Mr Fedorov have continued for the past month in Ukraine.

While Mr Fedorov did not say whether he would stand in an election, one recent poll has indicated the ex-minister could comfortably beat Mr Zelenskyy in a runoff vote, where the top two presidential candidates went head-to-head.

Protesters demand the reinstatement of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister last month. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

Mr Fedorov said Ukraine faced a "systemic crisis of governance".

"The old system lives by its own rules too often. It protects itself. It is scared of change," he said in his video address.

New Ukraine defence minister appointed

Mr Fedorov's statement came just hours after Mr Zelenskyy confirmed he had asked parliament to confirm new Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara in office on Wednesday.

The ex-minister has recently said he believed his reform of the Defence Ministry's procurement processes, responsible for purchasing billions of dollars of equipment, contributed to his sacking.

"Our people have long been ready for a different country," Mr Fedorov said in his address.

"Now, our state must become worthy of its people."

Mr Zelenskyy's office had no immediate comment on Mr Fedorov's address.

Reuters

World.title: Israeli military clears soldiers over Gaza strike that killed Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing in the April 2024 strike on a World Central Kitchen (WCK) convoy in Gaza, where Australian woman Zomi Frankcom was killed.

The IDF said it had concluded there were serious failures that led soldiers to falsely identify a Hamas fighter was travelling in the convoy, which prompted an attack that killed seven humanitarian workers.

The armed man travelling with the vehicles was a security guard "to protect it from seizure by armed actors in Gaza," the IDF said in its statement.

But it said the presence of that guard had not been flagged with the IDF prior to the convoy setting off, and the vehicles later took a different route to what had been coordinated prior with the military.

"Accordingly, and in light of the assessment that Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy before its arrival at the warehouse, the IDF mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles," it said.

The military argued it had tried to contact WCK about the incident, but did not hear back.

"Notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct."

Two commanders had already been stripped of their ranks as colonel and major, and a colonel, a major general and a brigadier general had also been reprimanded.

The ABC has contacted the Australian government for comment.

Just before the IDF announcement, Foreign Minister Penny Wong was marking World Humanitarian Day at an event in Parliament House in Canberra, where she launched an award in Ms Frankcom's honour in the presence of her family.

"I want to say to you that we will stand with you, and we will stand with you in years to come," Ms Wong said.

"I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli Government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues."

Zomi Frankcom volunteered with World Central Kitchen during the Black Summer bushfires. (Supplied: Kelly Eastwood)

Founder José Andrés said in the days following the attack "this was not just a bad luck situation where 'oops' we dropped the bomb in the wrong place".

"This was over 1.5, 1.8 kilometres, with a very defined humanitarian convoy that had signs in the top, in the roof, a very colourful logo that we are obviously very proud of," Mr Andrés said

"[It's] very clear who we are and what we do."

He described the IDF targeting each car, one-by-one, corralling the aid workers to the third car before it was ultimately struck.

Also killed in the strike were Palestinian Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, Damian Sobol from Poland, US-Canadian national Jacob Flickinger and John Chapman, James Henderson and James Kirby from the UK.

A 2024 Australian government review into the incident found the IDF strike was a result of "serious failures to follow procedures".

It found there was a "significant break down in situational awareness", however ultimately ruled the strike was "not knowingly or deliberately directed" against the WCK.

Seven people were killed in the strike. (AP: Abdel Kareem Hana)

On March 31, the family of Lalzawmi "Zomi" Frankcom commemorated two years since her killing.

"There hasn't been any kind of justice served or any movement with the case," her brother Mal Frankcom told Radio National Breakfast at the time

" It's going to be painful every year, but having that would provide some kind of comfort. "

The ABC has contacted WCK for comment.

Hind Rajab case prompts criminal probe

The IDF released details of five major investigations all at once on Wednesday afternoon, Israel time, and acknowledged for the first time it had opened fire on a car carrying five-year-old Hind Rajab.

The military said it would launch a criminal investigation into the January 2024 killing — a case which sparked worldwide outrage.

Hind was trapped in the wreckage of her family's car for hours, along with the bodies of seven family members, and had desperately called for help.

Paramedics who travelled to the scene were also attacked, killing two paramedics.

US holds talks in bid to salvage Gaza peace plan Jared Kushner and Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed putting a US general in charge of verifying Hamas's disarmaments, with Israel's military to remain place until that happens.

The bodies were recovered almost two weeks later.

The finding of the IDF investigation suggested the criminal probe would be limited in its scope.

"Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division."

Buried paramedics investigation also released

The IDF also said it had recommended a criminal investigation into an attack by the military on a convoy of Palestinian paramedics in Tel al-Sultan in March 2025, in which 15 people were killed.

The wreckage of the ambulances the group was travelling in, along with the remains of those killed, was buried by soldiers in a shallow mass grave.

At the time of the attack, the IDF claimed that the vehicles had been travelling without their emergency lights flashing.

Video recovered from a phone of one of the killed paramedics proved otherwise, recording the moments the convoy arrived at the scene and the lengthy assault by Israeli forces which followed.

Israeli authorities continue to insist six Hamas fighters were among those killed in the attack.

"The firing conducted during the incident raises a reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct," the IDF said.

The Palestinian Red Crescent Society has been contacted for comment.

Two investigations into the killing of Médecins Sans Frontières staff in Khan Younis in February 2024 and Gaza City November 2023 also cleared personnel of criminal wrongdoing.

World.title: Opera for the Dead and ocean-inspired works shine at Art Music Awards
World.content:
Melbourne-based experimental group Chamber Made has come out on top as the biggest winner of the 2026 Art Music Awards, held on 19 August in Melbourne.

The arts organisation picked up two awards: Excellence in Experimental Practice for its 2025 presentations and artist development activities, and the Victorian State Luminary Award for its incredible 35-year history of shaping Australian music and performance.

The ocean was a recurring theme for three of the evening’s winners.

Paul Stanhope's epic Mahāsāgar (the Hindi word for ocean) received the award for Work of the Year: Choral.

Alex Turley's the ocean's dream of itself for mezzo-soprano and orchestra won Work of the Year: Large Ensemble, while Dark Oceanography, created by Kate Milligan and a team of artists and climate science researchers was awarded Work of the Year: Electroacoustic/Sound Art.

Familiar names dominate Work of the Year awards

Other Work of the Year honours went to names familiar to ABC Classic audiences, including Anne Cawrse, whose Killing the Angel in the House, composed for 2022 ABC Young Performers Awards winner Eliza Shephard, won Work of the Year: Solo & Small Ensemble.

Other recipients included Nat Bartsch, Mindy Meng Wang and Monica Lim, as well as first-time winner Noemi Liba Friedman.

First Nations-led collaboration takes out Performance of the Year

Leading the Performance of the Year winners was nyilamum song cycles, a First Nations-led collaboration by Dr Lou Bennett AM and Paul Stanhope.

Performed by the Australian String Quartet and Yorta Yorta, Dja Dja Wurrung artist and academic Dr Bennett, it received the award for Performance of the Year: Classical & Experimental.

Nick Russoniello was awarded Performance of the Year: Soloist for his performance of his own composition, Air Mass Suite.

In Performance of the Year: Jazz & Improvised Music, The Cloud Maker took top honours for its performance of the work of the same name.

Leadership in Art Music celebrated with several awards

Internationally acclaimed Australian composer, educator and researcher, Professor Liza Lim AM, received the prestigious Richard Gill Award for Distinguished Services to Australian Music in recognition of her visionary contribution to Australian art music.

There were also several Luminary Awards, which recognised artists and organisations whose vision, leadership and commitment continue to shape Australian music across the country.

Musica Viva Australia was awarded the National Luminary Award (Organisation), and Daryl Buckley received the National Luminary Award (Individual).

The ceremony, organised by APRA AMCOS and the Australian Music Centre, was held on August 19 at The Timber Yard in Melbourne.

This year's awards were hosted by Namila Benson, with guest presenters Aura Go and Connor D'Netto, and music curation by Sia Ahmad.

List of winners and finalists

Work of the Year: Choral

Winner: Mahāsāgar: composed by Paul Stanhope with text by Rhys Halkidis, Steve Hawke, Michael Leunig, Cass Lynch, Alexander Maloof and Elizabeth Riddell. Performer: West Australian Symphony Orchestra and Chorus with Sara Macliver (soprano), Andrew Goodwin (tenor), and Asher Fisch (conductor) — publisher: Wise Music*

Adira Arenio and Agnus Dei: composed by Alice Chance with Kaylynn Zaro OAM and Noel Zaro OAM. Performer: Sydney Philharmonia Choirs VOX and Elizabeth Scott (conductor)

There is Music: composed by Stephen Leek with text by Jane Greenwood. Performer:Brisbane Chamber Choir

Vivemus Cantare: composed by Carl Crossin with text by James Wheldon Johnson, Walt Whitman and Carl Crossin. Performers: Adelaide Chamber Singers and Christie Anderson (conductor)

Work of the Year: Dramatic

Winner: Opera for the Dead: composed by Mindy Meng Wang and Monica Lim. Performers: Mindy Meng Wang, Monica Lim, Yu-Tien Lin, Nils Hobiger and Alexander Meagher

Hiroshima mon Amour: composed by Rósa Lind with text by Marguerite Duras. Performers: Bozzini Quartet and Chants Libre

Living Poems of the Sea: composed by Lyle Chan. Performer: Sally Walker (flutes, narration, percussion)

Pigeon Humongous: composed by Nicholas Roder. Performers: Nicholas Roder, Merinda Dias-Jayasinha, Lena Douglas, Lewis Coleman, Sydney Dance Company, and Harrison Ritchie-Jones (choreographer)

Work of the Year: Jazz & Improvised Music

Winner: When All Is Still and Quiet: composed by Nat Bartsch. Performers: VCA Secondary School Improvisation Ensemble & Chamber Choir — publisher: Origin Music Publishing

World.title: Graffiti 'wrongly' labelled antisemitic in Sydney spree, judge finds
World.content:
A man who admitted to a string of vandalism offences in Sydney's east did not act as an "antisemitic bigot" but was a "vandal for hire", and is not at risk of committing a serious terrorism offence, according to the state's highest court.

The NSW Supreme Court has dismissed an application by the State to place Mohommed Farhat under a year-long extended supervision order at the expiration of his jail sentence.

Had the application succeeded, it would have seen 55 strict conditions imposed on the 22-year-old, which would have been "highly restrictive" of his liberty.

Farhat pleaded guilty to 15 offences over the vandalism at Woollahra in November 2024, when vehicles were sprayed with slogans including "F*** Israel" and "PKK coming".

He was previously handed a sentence of one year and eight months with an expiry date in October 2026, and the State Parole Authority revoked his statutory parole due to a finding he posed a serious, identifiable risk to the safety of the community.

But Farhat has long claimed he was manipulated into the crimes and motivated by promises of money and drugs.

A Local Court judge previously said material before that court cast some doubt on the true motivation, but made a finding that a hatred of or prejudice against Jewish people was an aggravating factor.

The words "f*** Israel" were defaced on vehicles and property damaged, the judge said. (ABC News: Alison Xiao)

This week, Justice Desmond Fagan found that Farhat was "incited and directed" by another person to commit his crimes for a $4,000 payment and unspecified quantity of drugs.

He "did not intend to express hatred of Jews", the judge said in his reasons.

The judge also went on to find that the "f*** Israel" slogans were "objectively, crude expressions of political hostility to the state of Israel" and constituted a "curse against a foreign state".

"They are not antisemitic according to the ordinary understanding of that concept in the Australian community," Justice Fagan said.

"The fact that in this case the slogans were graffitied in a locality where a high proportion of residents may be Jewish does not imbue the curse with an antisemitic character."

Antisemitism definition criticised

Also in his reasons, Justice Fagan noted expert opinion before the court stated the definition of exactly what constitutes antisemitism was debated.

An analyst of middle eastern affairs, whose report was tendered by the Crown, made reference to a definition adopted by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).

But Justice Fagan said the IHRA's formulation did not assist him in Farhat's case and "does not reflect the established usage and understanding of the term 'antisemitic' in Australia".

"The IHRA core text is so verbose and imprecise that it could not realistically be attributed to the ordinary, reasonably informed member of the Australian public," he said.

The judge said he was not the first to criticise the "inept drafting" of the IHRA formulation, noting that in a submission to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, the Jewish Council of Australia (JCA) also criticised the wording and cited detailed critiques by others.

"Discussion of the IHRA wording and adoption of it by some institutions does not change the established meaning of a word that has been in use in the English language for 150 years," Justice Fagan said.

"The IHRA formulation propounds a concept different from that which 'antisemitism' has long been understood to describe and appropriates that word to the novel concept."

The court concluded that Australians who strongly disapprove of Israel's treatment of Palestinians "have freedom to express their views", and others who support Israel have the right not to listen, read or engage.

In Farhat's case, the judge found, the words "f*** Israel" were conveyed by defacing vehicles and damaging property, which meant the seriousness of the crime was "increased by its wantonness, vulgarity and intimidatory effect but not by any antisemitic implication".

'Label has been wrongly applied'

Justice Fagan said police statements and intelligence reports had "uniformly" described Farhat's spray-painting as antisemitic, and that was then taken up by the prosecution's submissions to the Local Court "without reflection or analysis".

Justice Fagan expressed the view, respectfully, that the Local Court judge made a legal error in finding that "f*** Israel" was an antisemitic phrase and reflective of hatred of prejudice towards Jewish people.

The characterisation of the graffiti as being antisemitic led to Farhat being treated differently under criminal law, Justice Fagan said.

"The label has been wrongly applied, injustice to the defendant has followed and the misconception has led to the State bringing these proceedings," he said.

In a letter to the Local Court, Farhat previously wrote that at the time of the vandalism, he was "lost in my ways", addicted to drugs, and did not realise the gravity of his actions or the effect on others, particularly the Jewish and Turkish communities.

He said visits from a Jewish community member had "really opened my eyes" and allowed him to look at things from the perspectives of others.

"At the time of my offending I did not understand the deep meaning of my actions and their impact," he wrote.

"My whole life was taken over by drugs and negative influences."

World.title: Kyrgios provisionally suspended after positive cocaine test in Spain
World.content:
Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has said he tested positive for cocaine on the Spanish island of Mallorca and has issued an apology.

In a statement on his Instagram, he announced he "made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it".

"I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me," Kyrgios said.

"Above all I'm sorry to the kids who follow me.

" I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed with myself. "

The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) issued a statement revealing Kyrgios had been "provisionally suspended" since August 4.

"31-year-old Kyrgios provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on 22 June 2026," it said.

"On 17 July 2026, a World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine."

"Kyrgios, who reached a career-high world singles ranking of 13 in October 2016, has the right to appeal the provisional suspension, but has not done so to date," the ITIA said.

"As with all Tennis Anti-Doping Programme cases, ITIA support is available to Kyrgios.

"While suspended, Kyrgios is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organised or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association."

Nick Kyrgios has been open with his struggles with mental health in the past, including with depression and suicidal ideation. (Reuters: Amr Alfiky)

Kyrgios explained the incident came in the context of years "of injuries … both physically and mentally".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined."

Kyrgios has spoken publicly about his previous struggles with mental health, telling the BBC in 2022 he struggled with alcohol and drug abuse, as well as depression and self-harm.

He has won seven ATP singles titles and the 2022 Australian Open doubles title, partnering with Thanasi Kokkinakis.

In July 2026, he lost in the first round of men's doubles at Wimbledon and later said it was probably his last appearance at the competition.

"I would probably say pretty confidently my last Wimbledon," Kyrgios said.

"It would be hard to see myself coming back here again and competing.

"That [2022] final was always going to be one of the better memories of my tennis career, but I just can't see myself getting back to anywhere near that level.

"I've always said I didn't choose tennis, tennis chose me," Kyrgios said.

"But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I've ever had to face.

" At times I've felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. "

He said the "good news" was his drug test failure and suspension "has given me a wake-up call" and said he would step away from social media and the public spotlight for the next 28 days.

"I'd ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly the privacy of my family," he said.

"I'm sorry.

"I'll do the work and come back better."

World.title: Oil prices spike after ships in Strait of Hormuz hit by fresh strikes
World.content:
Three ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz have been attacked in recent days, British maritime officials said.

The ships were struck by unknown projectiles, resulting in two casualties, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.

INTERCARGO, an association of cargo shipowners, reported that a sailor aboard the Liberian-flagged bulk carrier Minoan Dynasty was killed on Monday.

The Strait of Hormuz saw roughly a fifth of the world's oil pass through it before the war. (ABC News Graphics)

While hostilities between Iran and the United States have eased in recent weeks, a string of attacks on vessels passing through the strait has unsettled investors, pushing oil prices to a three-week high.

Brent crude futures jumped more than 3 per cent over the past week, to $US91.38 by 5:45pm AEST on Friday.

The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman is a vital shipping route for oil in the region.

Amid fresh strikes on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz and stalled peace talks, oil prices have spiked. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Uncertainty over passage through strait

Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, said on state media yesterday the strait will remain shut until the US meets the conditions of an interim deal signed between the two countries in June.

The conditions include the US lifting its own blockade, removing oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending military threats, he told parliament.

However, last week, Saudi Aramco, the world's top oil producer, resumed loading oil from inside the strait, eyeing Singapore and Malaysia as potential destinations.

Saudi Aramco resumed shipping through the strait last week. (AP: Hassan Ammar)

Despite Iran and the US not directly trading blows, energy prices have remained higher than pre-war levels while the roughly 500 million barrels that usually flow through the strait each month slowed to a trickle.

In a rally speech on Friday, US President Donald Trump said Americans should prepare for higher petrol prices as the war continues.

Shipping through the contested strait has slowed further in recent days, following similar attacks on vessels last week and talks between Iran and the US stalling.

Mr Trump said there are no talks planned between the two countries, and insisted the strait was open.

Donald Trump has repeatedly said throughout the war that the strait is open, saying the US controls the shipping routes. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

"The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated," he said on Truth Social yesterday.

" There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled with the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Naval Blockage remains in full force and effect. "

A ceasefire between Iran and the US expired on Monday, and Mr Trump said he would not be extending it.

The president also said that the US would claim the strait as a US territory after the war.

Trump says Strait of Hormuz to become US territory US President Donald Trump says he will soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, escalating his rhetoric over the vital waterway that carries a significant share of global oil supplies.

Trump upping the rhetoric

The strait is becoming a point of stress for the American president, as the ongoing Iran war becomes increasingly unpopular at home.

He recently threatened to bomb US ally Oman, saying: "If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the shit out of them", in an interview with Fox News.

Oman, whose coastline is a part of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran have been discussing opening the strait for weeks.

Six months into the conflict, 17 seafarers have died in the waterway according to the UN, with the number of ships passing through estimated to have dropped by roughly 90 per cent.

Many ships travel with their navigation and identification devices turned off to make them harder to attack.

"Seafarers are civilians and must never become targets or collateral victims of geopolitical conflicts," INTERCARGO said in a statement.

" One seafarer lost is one too many. "

ABC/Reuters

World.title: 'We are deeply sorry': Swans players break silence over alleged incident
World.content:
Five Sydney Swans players who were stood down for the rest of the season over breaches of club standards have issued an apology to their club, fans and the wider community.

In a statement on behalf of Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner, the players said they were "deeply sorry to everyone involved".

The players were banned by the Swans for breaches of standards and expected behaviour after they stayed out late drinking and brought women back to the team hotel after the game against Essendon on Sunday night.

"We know that our behaviour has fallen well short of the standards expected of us and the values of our club," they said.

The five said that they accepted the club's sanction and apologised for the impact on those involved.

Earlier in the day, the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending the five star players proved their commitment to upholding standards at the club.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Victorian detectives head to NSW

Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate the alleged incident.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault, and none of the banned players has been formally interviewed by police, according to the club.

Sponsors speak out

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Loading...

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

World.title: Politicians slam 'cruel tool' used to determine at-home aged care funding
World.content:
The federal government is standing by its controversial aged care algorithm, ignoring an offer from the opposition to provide a path through parliament to immediately fix the assessment process at the centre of hundreds of complaints.

Pressure is mounting on Labor over the algorithm after this week's Four Corners investigation, with the Coalition, Greens, independents and some Labor backbenchers, who did not want to be named, demanding the algorithm be either scrapped or urgently fixed.

Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston secured support when she introduced the bill in the Senate, aiming to overhaul what she labelled a "cruel tool" used to determine how much funding Support at Home recipients received by adding the ability for a human to override assessments.

While the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) involves input from clinicians filling out a questionnaire about the older person, controversially, assessors cannot override the algorithm's final decision on a participant's funding.

Anne Ruston says there is no evidence to prove the tool is working. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Experts, doctors and aged providers have all raised problems with this, including Australia's pre-eminent expert on health care algorithms, Kathy Eagar, who told Four Corners the algorithm needed to be completely ditched.

Last week, the Coalition criticised Labor for shutting down debate on the bill when it moved to the lower house.

"Labor could put human override back into aged care assessments today, by passing our private senator's bill in the House of Representatives," Senator Ruston said.

"Instead they blocked it even being debated, despite the fact it was supported by the Coalition, the Greens, and the crossbench."

Despite acknowledging there had been "confronting" cases, the government is resisting calls to allow human override, insisting the system is working quickly, fairly and has led to only a small number of review requests.

In the first five months of the algorithm's use, more than 1,000 people have asked for their outcome to be reviewed, with 207 people successfully receiving a reassessment.

Inside the aged care algorithm Four Corners reveals the fullest picture yet of the secretive algorithm affecting the lives of tens of thousands of older Australians and their families.

Labor has previously announced it would set up a new "escalation option" so people in "extenuating circumstances" could request their outcome be changed, after the ABC first exposed concerns about the algorithm in March.

Legislation to enact the escalation option has not yet been introduced.

The government is also reviewing the priority system used to determine how quickly someone receives their approved funding, but is not looking into the classification algorithm.

Senator Ruston said what had been announced was not good enough.

"We need more than a so-called 'rapid review' into just one aspect of the faceless algorithm," she said.

"Just as Professor Kathy Eagar AM says, the assessment algorithm is beyond repair, it needs throwing out and starting again.

"Until the government commits to that, older Australians cannot have confidence they will get the care they need."

Crossbenchers slam algorithm in joint statement

Monday's episode of Four Corners also prompted a Greens motion in the Senate calling on the government to replace the IAT with a system that "reinstate[s] the ability for human override".

The motion was backed by the Coalition and crossbenchers, including from the Greens, One Nation and independents.

"We know that this … tool is consistently under-assessing older people's care needs, and we know from the answers that the minister continues to give, that the government is not fully alive to the issue," Greens senator Penny Allman Payne told the Senate.

Senator Ruston said there was "not one piece of evidence" to suggest the tool was working.

"A cruel tool, that this government refuses to acknowledge, is causing older Australians to die unnecessarily," she said on Tuesday.

Independent MP Andrew Wilkie said his office had been contacted by "perplexed and distressed" older Australians struggling to understand the outcomes.

"If the minister thinks this tool is working well, he has his head in the sand," he said.

Monique Ryan is among the crossbenchers who fear the tool is inadequate. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Fellow independent Monique Ryan was worried the tool could amount to a repeat of Robodebt.

"The government's use of algorithms in aged care and the NDIS raises significant concerns around a repeat of the tragedies of Robodebt," she said.

"We can't allow that."

Minister defends tool to deliver 'predictability and consistency'

Despite the mounting pressure and saying the ABC had shared "confronting stories," Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler said he remained a "strong supporter" of the assessment framework.

"[The tool] didn't drop from the sky," he said.

"We're doing everything that we can to make sure this tool delivers the sort of predictability and consistency that the Royal Commission recommended."

In 2021, the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety recommended "a single assessment process based upon a common assessment framework and arrangements [be] followed by all assessors".

The Integrated Assessment Tool (recreated in these images) contains more than 500 questions. (Four Corners: Nick Wiggins)

Mr Butler said he supported a system "that gives confidence to Australians that no matter where they live, no matter what particular assessor organisation that they use, that their package level will reflect their level of need".

But former acting inspector-general of aged care Ian Yates said in his response that Mr Butler had "avoided" dealing with questions about the algorithm.

"The system as it's set up now, which was not as it was recommended by the Royal Commission, will continue to produce Audrey's and all the other cases that were featured in the Four Corners story," he said.

"It's about budgetary control rather than about person-centred care."

Mr Butler said there was still "a very significant role of clinical assessors through this process".

While the government said the IAT allowed for standardised decision making, some Labor MPs have told the ABC they were facing heat from constituents over the system and had raised concerns with Aged Care Minister Sam Rae.

Government follows up cases of participants who spoke out

The Four Corners episode aired a story of a frail 96-year-old who was rejected from receiving more funding to help her pay for the rising cost of in-home care because of an outcome reached by the algorithm.

Sean Dorney was a roaming ABC reporter. Now, just getting out of bed is a struggle A long-time ABC reporter is one of nearly 100,000 Australians waiting on a crucial aged-care assessment.

Under questioning from Liberal Senator Richard Colbeck on Tuesday, Labor's Penny Wong said Audrey Staniland's inability to get more funding sounded "extremely distressing" and the minister had asked the department to look into her case.

One of the other Australians at the centre of the expose on Monday, Sean Dorney, has been told after eight months he would be reassessed for more funding after his decision to speak out.

In the first five months of the algorithm's use, more than 1,000 people have asked for their outcome to be reviewed, with 207 people successful.

World.title: Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m of CBA shares amid separation from wife
World.content:
NationalCBD Opinion Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m of CBA shares amid separation from wife John Buckley CBD columnist August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm

August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Executives sell shares in their own companies all the time. So when Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn offloaded about $8.4 million worth of shares last week, we didn’t think much of it. But that was before we knew Comyn and his wife, Lucy, are working through the terms of their separation, which CBD brought word of on Tuesday, after the Commonwealth Bank confirmed the couple had split. Commonwealth Bank chief Matt Comyn presents the bank’s full year 2026 results. Nic Long The share disclosure, released to the market on August 14, showed Comyn acquired a tick over 30,000 shares as a result of vested equity earned as part of his remuneration. Then there were two tranches of shares sold: The first tranche of 30,006 shares sold at $168.18 per share, worth a little over $5 million. The second lot of 20,091 shares went at $168.80, worth about $3.4 million. All up, the share movement leaves Comyn’s direct shareholding about the same as it was the day before, and is not out of step with his previous share sales, which have occurred at least once a year since 2022. A Commonwealth Bank spokesman declined to comment on whether Comyn’s share sale this month was related to his separation.



But our guess is the sale, the second tranche of which was jointly held by Comyn and his wife as beneficiaries of a trust, freed up a helpful chunk of cash for whatever costs are racked up through the separation, and, of course, may make it easier for the couple to split their assets. Another Pauline whisperer It was only June when we last brought word of the frenzy among corporates to find so-called “Pauline whisperers” to cosy up to One Nation as the party rises in the polls. Well, it looks like business is good enough for those who already have a line into One Nation leader Pauline Hanson to flaunt their access. One lobbyist who has since made the pitch for those betting that Hanson’s popularity will hold out until at least 2028 is Jannette Cotterell, who set up her lobby shop Executive Counsel Australia back in 2008 following a five-year stint at CT Group, formerly known as Crosby Textor.



Cotterell describes herself as non-partisan, and in a post to LinkedIn felt it necessary to declare “engagement does not equal endorsement”. We bet! When reached on Tuesday, Cotterell was quick to have a crack at us over the sausagefest of names that populated our last column item on the matter. She was also quick to take the opportunity to pump up her own tyres. But we’ll spare you the marketing material. Cotterral’s name joins a string of others who have been bandied about in political circles as possible One Nation relationship brokers. So far we’ve heard the name of Gina Rinehart’s media minder James Radford come up. So too former Nationals deputy campaign director and conservative lobbyist Michael Kauter. Also: Scott Mitchell, who spent five years as the federal director of the Nationals before setting up his own lobby shop. We’re sure they’re freshening up their pitch decks. Life after Ley Former opposition leader Sussan Ley’s ex-spinner Liam Jones may be having a little trouble letting go of his old life, as CBD brought word of last week.



But it looks like Ley’s former chief of staff Dean Shachar has had no such trouble moving on – to a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, no less. On Wednesday, Shachar was quick to brag about his rendezvous with Albanese in Canberra in a post to LinkedIn, after the PM was able to squeeze in some time in the diary to hear all about Shachar’s new employer, the retail share trading platform, Superhero. But apparently it wasn’t just Albo and Shachar there to chew the fat. Also present were the company’s co-founders, chief executive John Winters and chief technology officer Wayne Baskin, who presented Albo with a Hawthorn Football Club jersey. The Superhero founders were simply flogging their own wares, given the company is a back-of-jersey sponsor. But who knows, given Albo’s approach to politics, the Hawks may be in with a shot to win over a new supporter. The PM wasn’t the only one who had to sit through the pitch. Winters and Shachar were also seen at Aussies on Thursday morning in talks with Chris Taylor, the newly minted chief of staff to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. The Superhero guys also made overtures to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s office on Wednesday, CBD hears, and met with several Coalition MPs through the week.



Airwallex Cafe It would seem no idea is too corny for the Airwallex marketing team. There was the financial start-up’s bizarre co-sponsorship of a function on a yacht called “Mischief”. Then the company’s sponsorship of Essendon Football Club. Now the company has set up a pop-up cafe. But our guess is any idea that distracts from the audit announced by the nation’s financial crimes agency AUSTRAC this year is probably considered a good one. “Yeah, I mean look, it’s just a great opportunity where we know people are in town candidly, and like the majority of people here are customers,” the company’s Australia and New Zealand boss James Teodorini said on Wednesday. “We’re lucky – I was just speaking to someone who’s been a customer for nine years and they were like, want to come down and say hi. “Um, it’s an opportunity while people are in town. Not to go and necessarily do this versus that, but just talk about who we are.” Nice one.



The cafe was set up around the corner from the ICC in Sydney, where Airwallex’s rival payments company, Stripe, was hosting an event of its own. As far as stunts go, this has to be among the lamest. World.title: Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors Ben Cubby and Emily Kowal Updated August 19, 2026 — 9:09pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scots College has hit back against claims from parents that the prestigious private school had reacted poorly to the ongoing sexual assault scandal because the families of some of the boys who have been charged were financial donors to the school. The students – a 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys – were charged with aggravated sexual assault after an alleged attack on a girl in a Bondi Junction laneway on July 22. Some parents told the Herald they were concerned the school was downplaying the seriousness of the incident because of financial donations previously made by families of two of the three boys, who cannot be legally identified. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s “active and continuing” handling of the crisis, and said he intended to remain in his role until his planned retirement at the end of next year amid calls for his resignation.



“The suggestion that the college is shielding any student because of a family donation is false,” Lambert, who has held the title of school principal for 19 years, said in a statement. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s handling of the crisis. “Donations have no bearing whatsoever on decisions concerning student welfare, attendance or discipline. “The same standards apply to every student, with each case considered on its facts and in accordance with law, not according to family circumstances or public pressure.” One concerned parent with a student at the private boys’ school said the anger [among parents] was palpable.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Scots College briefs boys as young as 10 on sexual assault allegations as council backs principal “The accusation is horrifying and, of course, we worry about the effect on our boy, anybody would. The students will be tarred with same brush. Honestly, I think they would have had their enrolment looked into already if they hadn’t donated,” the parent said. Another parent said the school had failed to substantially address her questions about culture in relation to the alleged assault on July 22 and previous incidents at the elite institution. “I’m appalled at how the school has responded,” said the parent with a boy in the same year group as the three boys charged with sex offences. “It’s how you react when these things happen that define you. And the way that the school is reacting right now is appalling personally as a parent, as a woman, as a human being. You don’t have to be a woman.



“It’s just not the culture I want my son in.” The question of financial donations is considered sensitive by many in the school community because Scots College is heavily dependent on cash gifts from parents, with more than 400 names listed on the school’s donations register. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations. Alex Donnini Philanthropic giving generally yields the school about $4 million to $6 million a year, according to its financial disclosures. However, much larger sums have been obtained from the school community to fund capital works programs. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations, including a gift of more than $12 million from Cunningham, a former student, management consultant and honorary consul general of Barbados in Australia.



Three other families gave more than $1 million each towards the building’s construction, while another 81 families, trusts and foundations kicked in tens of thousands each to get the project off the ground, according to school records. The median income of households with children at the Bellevue Hill school was $336,000 in 2024, and fees can be among the highest in the nation at more than $50,000 a year. Parents and former students said they could only speak anonymously of their concerns about the school’s culture because they were worried about a backlash against their children. Lambert said their fears were unfounded. “The college does not take disciplinary action against students because a parent or former student has lawfully expressed a concern or opinion about the college,” he said.



“We expect genuine concerns to be raised directly with the college so they can be answered, while every member of our community must protect young people’s privacy and welfare and respect the legal process.” It is not the first time Lambert has been forced to defend the school against claims of sexual assault by Scots College boys. In 2021, several Sydney private schools, including Scots, faced allegations raised in an online petition – launched by former Kambala student Chanel Contos – that students had assaulted young women. Related Article Opinion

Crime When the accused in sex crimes are children, school leaders must wake up to a toxic culture Chanel Contos Founder of Teach Us Consent Women described waking up naked at parties after passing out due to intoxication, with male peers penetrating them.



Other students said they were physically forced to perform oral sex on a male while intoxicated, sometimes while the boy’s friends were present or filming the incident. Lambert said at the time: “It is a wake-up call for us all.” When asked on Wednesday whether the college would be reviewing its education around consent and behavioural expectations of students in light of the assault allegations, he said: “We do not accept that charges against individual students establish a failure of education, or that a difference between our methods and others’ preferences constitutes a deficiency. “Consent, dignity, respectful relationships, self-control and personal responsibility are taught age-appropriately and cumulatively throughout a student’s years at Scots, grounded in Christian conviction.” With Chris Harris, Riley Walter and Natassia Chrysanthos



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I’m sorry to the kids who follow me’: Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis
World.content:
Updated SportTennisDrugs in sport ‘I’m sorry to the kids who follow me’: Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis Marc McGowan Updated August 19, 2026 — 8:41pm ,first published 6:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Controversial Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has taken full responsibility for making a “huge mistake” and will briefly step away from the limelight after testing positive for cocaine. The International Tennis Integrity Agency announced on Wednesday night (AEST) that it had provisionally suspended Kyrgios under the tennis anti-doping program. He has so far not appealed the decision. Nick Kyrgios is a former world No.13 who reached the 2022 men’s singles final at Wimbledon. Marijan Murat/Picture Alliance via Getty Images The 31-year-old provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on June 22 before a World Anti-Doping Agency-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, on July 17. Kyrgios lost in the first round at Mallorca to fellow Australian Adam Walton. His provisional suspension started on August 4.



In a statement posted to his Instagram story on Wednesday, Kyrgios apologised for his actions and said he would take a break from social media and public life to “focus on getting myself right”. “I wanted you to hear this from me first. I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” Kyrgios posted. Loading “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it. I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets, and I’m deeply disappointed in myself. “I’m not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I’ve been. The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.



Related Article Wimbledon Kyrgios drama as he bids Wimbledon farewell; doubt surrounds Serena “My body hasn’t been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined. “I’ve always said I didn’t choose tennis – tennis chose me. But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to face. At times, I’ve felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. “However, the good news is that this has given me a wake-up call. For the next 28 days, I’ll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right. “I’d ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly, the privacy of my family. I’m sorry. I’ll do the work and come back better.”



Nick Kyrgios’ apology on his official Instagram account. Instagram Kyrgios revealed in a frank social media post four years ago that, during one of his “darkest periods” around the time of the 2019 Australian Open, he resorted to self-harming and substance abuse while experiencing depression. “I was having suicidal thoughts and was literally struggling to get out of bed, let alone play in front of millions. I was lonely, depressed, negative, abusing alcohol, drugs, pushed away family and friends,” Kyrgios posted at the time. “I felt as if I couldn’t talk or trust anyone.” Kyrgios has been one of Australia’s highest-profile athletes since his titanic upset of Spanish tennis legend Rafael Nadal as a 19-year-old to reach the Wimbledon quarter-finals in 2019.



The former world No.13’s colourful and outspoken persona and habit for courting controversy – on and off the court – have made him one of the most polarising but undoubtedly popular players on tour. After being routinely labelled an underachiever for years, Kyrgios produced a career-best season in 2022 that included making his maiden and only grand slam singles final at Wimbledon, where he won the first set before losing to Novak Djokovic. He also advanced to the US Open quarter-finals two months later. However, repeated injury setbacks cruelled Kyrgios’ hopes of building on that success, starting with a lateral meniscus tear and a cyst in his left knee that caused him to withdraw from the 2023 Australian Open. Knee and wrist surgeries played a major role in him playing only 10 singles matches across the past four years, which has seen his ranking tumble to No.919.



This masthead has contacted Kyrgios’ management. Retired British player Dan Evans received a one-year ban in 2017 after testing positive to cocaine. Evans avoided the maximum four-year sanction because the International Tennis Federation said at the time that cocaine was not performance enhancing and the drug was taken out of competition. An off-the-plan apartment buyer in a huge riverfront project has criticised an “appalling” lack of communication from the developer, amid renewed questions about the project’s future. Teneriffe Banks at Skyring Terrace in Teneriffe is slated to comprise five towers with 212 apartments, a Kimpton Hotel, shops, restaurants, bars, and an extension of the riverwalk. Kokoda Property Group is behind the project, which is expected to cost about $1.5 billion. An earlier plan for Teneriffe Banks had included a skybridge linking two towers, but the feature was scrapped during a redesign. Kokoda Property Group In July it emerged that one of its entities, Riverd Pty Ltd, had gone into administration, owing more than $90 million.



The developer was adamant it would have no impact on Teneriffe Banks. After media reports suggested the administration cast a cloud over the project’s funding, Kokoda Property Group wrote to buyers on July 27 to dismiss concerns. The Teneriffe Banks site on Skyring Terrace has been cleared, but construction work was yet to begin on Wednesday. William Davis A spokesperson did not say what Riverd Pty Ltd – which had previously been called Kokoda Property Group Pty Ltd – did when contacted by this masthead on Wednesday evening, only that it was not relevant to the development. “We have obviously a great deal of entities, given that we’re a property developer and have multiple different projects,” they said.



“[Teneriffe Banks’] funding is secured … everything is tracking along really nicely.” An artist’s impression of the $1.5 billion Teneriffe Banks development. Kokoda Property Group The spokesperson added that the first stage of development remained on track for 2028, with construction to begin late this year or early 2027. But a buyer who put forward a 10 per cent deposit on a $4.8 million three-bedroom apartment in the complex in late 2024 said communication had not been good enough, and anything that could delay construction was a significant concern due to a sunset clause in her contract. The clause could allow the developer to terminate its sale agreement and refund her deposit if construction criteria weren’t met within 3½ years of the deal being signed.





A second buyer at Teneriffe Banks said they were not overly concerned by recent developments, and believed their apartment would be delivered. The Kokoda spokesperson added that the sprawling marina shown in marketing material would absolutely be built as pictured, despite questions previously being raised about its approval process. World.title: Over 100 olympic pools of ‘bin juice’ from this Perth tip is seeping into the ground
World.content:
NationalWAWaste Over 100 olympic pools of ‘bin juice’ from this Perth tip is seeping into the ground Alastair Kirkby Indigo Lemay-Conway and August 19, 2026 — 8:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is no secret that the smell from a landfill stinks. But the real concern is what is beneath the surface. At Tamala Park Waste Facility, situated in Perth’s northern suburbs, the answer to that is leachate, and a lot of it. Tamala Park opened in 1991. Mindarie Regional Council Tamala Park landfill is run by the Mindarie Regional Council and has accepted the household waste of 800,000 Perth homes for 35 years. The council is made up of seven local governments and was due to reach the end of its operational life around 2028, however, an excessive buildup of liquid waste is now threatening to derail those closure plans.



As of October 2024, data shows there were 167 olympic sized swimming pools worth of leachate accumulated at the bottom of the tip. Without any removal methods in place, that number is expected to have risen. The situation has now triggered formal regulatory enforcement. Western Australia’s Department of Water and Environmental Regulation issued the regional council an official Environmental Protection Notice on August 3. The notice requires the MRC to provide a detailed and accurate determination of the leachate levels as well as a leachate removal plan, and they have 30 days to do it. The EPN also requires the council to improve its landfill gas management, provide updated landfill closure planning, and undertake additional technical investigations. Western Sydney University science professor Ian Wright has been a water scientist for 30 years and describes leachate as the liquid often seen at the bottom of household bins.



“Leachate is the liquid that builds up in rotting rubbish. So a lot of people might have seen it if your garbage bin with lots of food and kitchen scraps has been left in the house, and you perhaps went away for a few days,” he said. Western Sydney University science professor Ian Wright. “It’s often a tea-coloured liquid that stinks, and it’s basically decomposing waste, and it’s chemically full of lots and lots of contaminants.” Wright said the 167 olympic pools worth of leachate was a significant amount to be accumulated at the bottom of any tip and that it was “a major issue” for groundwater health. The landfill is only partially lined and the MRC’s recent request to install a piggyback liner and create a leachate management area in the northern portion of the tip – closest to the nearby residential homes – was rejected by DWER at the beginning of August.



A DWER spokesperson said the high leachate levels was one of the reasons behind the decision. “Highly elevated leachate levels were a significant consideration during the assessment of a piggyback liner and leachate management area,” they said. “Following detailed technical assessment, DWER concluded that the proposed works would generate additional leachate and would not adequately address the existing leachate, odour and groundwater issues at the site.” The regulatory body also acknowledged there are ongoing investigations into groundwater contamination at the site but that there is currently a “low” risk to human health and the broader environment. Wright said he was “very surprised” the landfill hadn’t been fully lined as to prevent groundwater contamination of the nearby Gnangara aquifer, which provides almost half of all the water used in the Perth metropolitan area each year.



“As soon as I heard about this case study, my mind went straight to: could this be in any way a threat or a risk to Perth’s groundwater? Because the Gnangara sand aquifer is right on the edge of this area,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Waste Plans trashed: Where to dump one-third of Perth’s household waste? “It’s easy for waste from something like this landfill to move through sand down to the aquifer, so as to contaminate the groundwater.” Wright said groundwater contamination wasn’t the only risk associated with leachate buildup as methane can also be a byproduct of the breakdown of household waste. “With all this rotting landfill, and particularly the organic wastes that start breaking down, because it’s sealed under metres and metres of landfill, it starts breaking down away from oxygen, and that can create the perfect environment for methane,” he said.



Methane presents a threefold-hazard for Wright: it’s a bad greenhouse gas, it stinks, and it’s explosive. “The thing with methane is it stinks. There are suburbs growing around here, and I’m actually very surprised there isn’t a larger buffer around this landfill for the suburban development,” he said. “Methane can also blow up, and one of the concerns in the auditor’s report is that it is an explosive gas, and the gas coming from this rotting waste underground can actually rise through the surface, through the layers of soil and landfill, and if there are buildings nearby, it can sometimes rise into them. “It can even go through concrete slabs, concrete is a porous material. It can build up in buildings, and yes, it can build up to explosive levels.” Wright said he would encourage the MRC to embrace the residents and their concerns around the leachate.



“Outrage can ferment with something like this,” he said. Resident Mary O’Byrne has been championing the odour issue at Tamala Park for years and is now calling on government officials to step in. “My concern is the groundwater, what’s happening to that, and how it affects residents,” she said. “I want a government inquiry into how this place is run. I want to know why, for three and a half years, they didn’t evaporate the leachate.” Mary O’Byrne is a resident who has been campaigning against the odour and environmental concerns at Tamala Park Waste Facility. 9 News Perth



Wright said he felt like the council was trying to do their best to mitigate the problems that likely began long before most councillors were in their roles. “I can see that the council is trying their absolute best to take account of all those decisions in the past, and manage it best for locals, but there’s lots of challenges here,” he said. A spokesperson for the MRC said they were taking the management of the landfill and the protection of the surrounding environment “extremely seriously”. “Elevated levels of leachate within the landfill is an issue that both MRC and the regulator have been aware of for some time. We share DWER’s concerns on this matter and are committed to finding a viable and lasting solution,” they said. “MRC presented this information to the regulator voluntarily, and we have worked with the Department for several years to monitor and manage the site’s environmental risks and to ensure the landfill can be safely and successfully rehabilitated.”



But they said they couldn’t quantify the amount of leachate contained within the landfill and that it was a focus of their work in the coming months. “We continue to deploy measures on site to control the amount of leachate generated, to prioritise the capping of open landfill areas, and to optimise odour management.” Wright warns however that it will take many decades to manage the leachate issues on the site. “Grandchildren of people living in this area will still have to deal with this,” he said.

World.title: Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m worth of CBA shares amid separation from his wife
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m worth of CBA shares amid separation from his wife Fiona Byrne and John Buckley August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Executives sell shares in their own companies all the time. So when Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn offloaded about $8.4 million worth of shares last week, we didn’t think much of it. But that was before we knew that Comyn and his wife, Lucy, were working through the terms of their separation, which CBD brought word of on Tuesday, after the Commonwealth Bank confirmed the couple had split. Commonwealth Bank CEO Matt Comyn has separated from his wife. Dominic Lorrimer The disclosure, which was released to the market on August 14, showed Comyn acquired a tick over 30,000 shares as a result of vested equity earned as part of his remuneration. Then there were two tranches of shares sold. The first tranche sold 30,006 shares at $168.18 per share, worth a little over $5 million. The second sold 20,091 shares at $168.80, worth about $3.4 million. All up, the share movement leaves Comyn’s direct shareholding about the same as it was the day before, and is not out of step with his previous share sales, which have occurred at least once a year since 2022. A Commonwealth Bank spokesman declined to comment on whether Comyn’s share sale this month was related to his separation.



But our guess is the sale, the second tranche of which was jointly held by Comyn and his wife as beneficiaries of a trust, freed up a helpful chunk of cash for whatever costs are racked up through the separation, and, of course, may make it easier for the couple to split their assets. No end in sight for Hughesy’s Liberal spruiking Politically activated comedian Dave Hughes is ramping up his Liberals spruiking tour and will join Williamstown candidate Paul Lindemann for a Pub Talks event next month. While he continues to rule out ever standing for a seat and is not a Liberal Party member, Hughesy is in full campaign mode, and the more criticism he attracts for his anti-Labor rants and corruption-busting call-outs, the more he is leaning into his political epiphany. Dave Hughes has been making headlines for his criticism of Labor. Simon Schluter



He’s a preacher who has found his pulpit and is relentless. He’s had plenty of experience over the years doing press roll-outs for TV shows and his stand-up tours, so in some ways, pumping up Jess Wilson and the Libs’ tyres is just another type of publicity push for the former radio host. Related Article Victorian election Dave Hughes to campaign for Liberals in Victorian election “I think the Liberals are our best bet right now,” Hughesy told CBD last week when confirming he would back Wilson in November’s state election. Hughesy will be unleashed with Lindemann at a yet-to-be-revealed location on September 16. This is no laughing matter. “I’ve known him a long time, ” Lindemann said of his Hughesy connection when CBD called.



“I used to work in real estate in Altona and he was always looking for a property in the area. He never actually bought anything off me, but he was always enquiring. “I’ve been trying to nail him down for a while and finally he said, ‘All right, I’ll do it’.” Meanwhile, in an inevitable coming together of celebrities piping up about politics, Hughesy turned up where else but on Karl Stefanovic’s podcast on Wednesday night. Maggie T mementos up for grabs For decades, Maggie Tabberer was a beacon of elegance for Australian women – not to mention a two-time winner of the Gold Logie for her TV work – and now pieces of her legacy are up for grabs.



After her death in December 2024, Tabberer’s family are putting a curated collection of her jewellery under the hammer with Shapiro Auctioneers. It is the third auction of items from Tabberer’s sizeable estate. Fashion doyenne Maggie Tabberer. Of the 20 lots, CBD took note of the set of Cartier pens, one with the name Maggie T engraved on it, and a YSL wrist cuff with Maggie fashioned across it. It was custom-made for Tabberer by YSL. What’s the saying about what’s in a name? Other featured pieces include a strand of South Sea pearls, a long 18ct gold curb link necklace with nine charms which has an estimate of $20,000-25,000, and a set of Gucci pens. The distinctive necklace, with one of the charms being a large gold M, was one of Tabberer’s favourite jewellery pieces, CBD was informed. Other items for sale include rings, bracelets, watches and necklaces. As would be expected from Tabberer, it is a classy collection.



“She loved her life and she loved everything she owned,” Brooke Tabberer, Maggie’s daughter, told CBD. “They say every picture tells a story and there are many a story to each piece in the collection that is being offered. She was a lady of great style and good luck to the new owners.” A set of Cartier pens, one with the name ‘Maggie T’ engraved on the cap, owned by Maggie Tabberer is going to auction with Shapiro Auctioneers. Shapiro Auctioneers/supplied The pieces will be sold via online auction. Bidding is under way and will close on August 25. There was no sign, however, of Tabberer’s Gold Logies, which remain with her family.
