World.title: Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWEducation Scots College denies shielding boys because parents were donors Ben Cubby and Emily Kowal Updated August 19, 2026 — 9:09pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scots College has hit back against claims from parents that the prestigious private school had reacted poorly to the ongoing sexual assault scandal because the families of some of the boys who have been charged were financial donors to the school. The students – a 13-year-old boy and two 14-year-old boys – were charged with aggravated sexual assault after an alleged attack on a girl in a Bondi Junction laneway on July 22. Some parents told the Herald they were concerned the school was downplaying the seriousness of the incident because of financial donations previously made by families of two of the three boys, who cannot be legally identified. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s “active and continuing” handling of the crisis, and said he intended to remain in his role until his planned retirement at the end of next year amid calls for his resignation.



“The suggestion that the college is shielding any student because of a family donation is false,” Lambert, who has held the title of school principal for 19 years, said in a statement. Scots College principal Dr Ian Lambert defended the school’s handling of the crisis. “Donations have no bearing whatsoever on decisions concerning student welfare, attendance or discipline. “The same standards apply to every student, with each case considered on its facts and in accordance with law, not according to family circumstances or public pressure.” One concerned parent with a student at the private boys’ school said the anger [among parents] was palpable.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Scots College briefs boys as young as 10 on sexual assault allegations as council backs principal “The accusation is horrifying and, of course, we worry about the effect on our boy, anybody would. The students will be tarred with same brush. Honestly, I think they would have had their enrolment looked into already if they hadn’t donated,” the parent said. Another parent said the school had failed to substantially address her questions about culture in relation to the alleged assault on July 22 and previous incidents at the elite institution. “I’m appalled at how the school has responded,” said the parent with a boy in the same year group as the three boys charged with sex offences. “It’s how you react when these things happen that define you. And the way that the school is reacting right now is appalling personally as a parent, as a woman, as a human being. You don’t have to be a woman.



“It’s just not the culture I want my son in.” The question of financial donations is considered sensitive by many in the school community because Scots College is heavily dependent on cash gifts from parents, with more than 400 names listed on the school’s donations register. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations. Alex Donnini Philanthropic giving generally yields the school about $4 million to $6 million a year, according to its financial disclosures. However, much larger sums have been obtained from the school community to fund capital works programs. The school’s $60 million John Cunningham Student Centre, built in the style of a Scottish baronial castle, was in large part funded by donations, including a gift of more than $12 million from Cunningham, a former student, management consultant and honorary consul general of Barbados in Australia.



Three other families gave more than $1 million each towards the building’s construction, while another 81 families, trusts and foundations kicked in tens of thousands each to get the project off the ground, according to school records. The median income of households with children at the Bellevue Hill school was $336,000 in 2024, and fees can be among the highest in the nation at more than $50,000 a year. Parents and former students said they could only speak anonymously of their concerns about the school’s culture because they were worried about a backlash against their children. Lambert said their fears were unfounded. “The college does not take disciplinary action against students because a parent or former student has lawfully expressed a concern or opinion about the college,” he said.



“We expect genuine concerns to be raised directly with the college so they can be answered, while every member of our community must protect young people’s privacy and welfare and respect the legal process.” It is not the first time Lambert has been forced to defend the school against claims of sexual assault by Scots College boys. In 2021, several Sydney private schools, including Scots, faced allegations raised in an online petition – launched by former Kambala student Chanel Contos – that students had assaulted young women. Related Article Opinion

Crime When the accused in sex crimes are children, school leaders must wake up to a toxic culture Chanel Contos Founder of Teach Us Consent Women described waking up naked at parties after passing out due to intoxication, with male peers penetrating them.



Other students said they were physically forced to perform oral sex on a male while intoxicated, sometimes while the boy’s friends were present or filming the incident. Lambert said at the time: “It is a wake-up call for us all.” When asked on Wednesday whether the college would be reviewing its education around consent and behavioural expectations of students in light of the assault allegations, he said: “We do not accept that charges against individual students establish a failure of education, or that a difference between our methods and others’ preferences constitutes a deficiency. “Consent, dignity, respectful relationships, self-control and personal responsibility are taught age-appropriately and cumulatively throughout a student’s years at Scots, grounded in Christian conviction.” With Chris Harris, Riley Walter and Natassia Chrysanthos



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I’m sorry to the kids who follow me’: Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis
World.content:
Updated SportTennisDrugs in sport ‘I’m sorry to the kids who follow me’: Kyrgios tests positive for cocaine, faces lengthy ban from tennis Marc McGowan Updated August 19, 2026 — 8:41pm ,first published 6:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Controversial Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has taken full responsibility for making a “huge mistake” and will briefly step away from the limelight after testing positive for cocaine. The International Tennis Integrity Agency announced on Wednesday night (AEST) that it had provisionally suspended Kyrgios under the tennis anti-doping program. He has so far not appealed the decision. Nick Kyrgios is a former world No.13 who reached the 2022 men’s singles final at Wimbledon. Marijan Murat/Picture Alliance via Getty Images The 31-year-old provided a sample during an ATP 250 event in Mallorca, Spain, on June 22 before a World Anti-Doping Agency-accredited laboratory confirmed the presence of benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, on July 17. Kyrgios lost in the first round at Mallorca to fellow Australian Adam Walton. His provisional suspension started on August 4.



In a statement posted to his Instagram story on Wednesday, Kyrgios apologised for his actions and said he would take a break from social media and public life to “focus on getting myself right”. “I wanted you to hear this from me first. I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” Kyrgios posted. Loading “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it. I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets, and I’m deeply disappointed in myself. “I’m not going to make excuses, but I do want to give some context about where I’ve been. The last couple of years of injuries have taken a huge toll on me, both physically and mentally.



Related Article Wimbledon Kyrgios drama as he bids Wimbledon farewell; doubt surrounds Serena “My body hasn’t been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined. “I’ve always said I didn’t choose tennis – tennis chose me. But letting go of something that has been my whole life is one of the hardest things I’ve ever had to face. At times, I’ve felt helpless and alone. None of that excuses what I did. “However, the good news is that this has given me a wake-up call. For the next 28 days, I’ll be stepping away from social media and public life while I focus on getting myself right. “I’d ask that people respect my privacy during that time, and most importantly, the privacy of my family. I’m sorry. I’ll do the work and come back better.”



Nick Kyrgios’ apology on his official Instagram account. Instagram Kyrgios revealed in a frank social media post four years ago that, during one of his “darkest periods” around the time of the 2019 Australian Open, he resorted to self-harming and substance abuse while experiencing depression. “I was having suicidal thoughts and was literally struggling to get out of bed, let alone play in front of millions. I was lonely, depressed, negative, abusing alcohol, drugs, pushed away family and friends,” Kyrgios posted at the time. “I felt as if I couldn’t talk or trust anyone.” Kyrgios has been one of Australia’s highest-profile athletes since his titanic upset of Spanish tennis legend Rafael Nadal as a 19-year-old to reach the Wimbledon quarter-finals in 2019.



The former world No.13’s colourful and outspoken persona and habit for courting controversy – on and off the court – have made him one of the most polarising but undoubtedly popular players on tour. After being routinely labelled an underachiever for years, Kyrgios produced a career-best season in 2022 that included making his maiden and only grand slam singles final at Wimbledon, where he won the first set before losing to Novak Djokovic. He also advanced to the US Open quarter-finals two months later. However, repeated injury setbacks cruelled Kyrgios’ hopes of building on that success, starting with a lateral meniscus tear and a cyst in his left knee that caused him to withdraw from the 2023 Australian Open. Knee and wrist surgeries played a major role in him playing only 10 singles matches across the past four years, which has seen his ranking tumble to No.919.



This masthead has contacted Kyrgios’ management. Retired British player Dan Evans received a one-year ban in 2017 after testing positive to cocaine. Evans avoided the maximum four-year sanction because the International Tennis Federation said at the time that cocaine was not performance enhancing and the drug was taken out of competition. An off-the-plan apartment buyer in a huge riverfront project has criticised an “appalling” lack of communication from the developer, amid renewed questions about the project’s future. Teneriffe Banks at Skyring Terrace in Teneriffe is slated to comprise five towers with 212 apartments, a Kimpton Hotel, shops, restaurants, bars, and an extension of the riverwalk. Kokoda Property Group is behind the project, which is expected to cost about $1.5 billion. An earlier plan for Teneriffe Banks had included a skybridge linking two towers, but the feature was scrapped during a redesign. Kokoda Property Group In July it emerged that one of its entities, Riverd Pty Ltd, had gone into administration, owing more than $90 million.



The developer was adamant it would have no impact on Teneriffe Banks. After media reports suggested the administration cast a cloud over the project’s funding, Kokoda Property Group wrote to buyers on July 27 to dismiss concerns. The Teneriffe Banks site on Skyring Terrace has been cleared, but construction work was yet to begin on Wednesday. William Davis A spokesperson did not say what Riverd Pty Ltd – which had previously been called Kokoda Property Group Pty Ltd – did when contacted by this masthead on Wednesday evening, only that it was not relevant to the development. “We have obviously a great deal of entities, given that we’re a property developer and have multiple different projects,” they said.



“[Teneriffe Banks’] funding is secured … everything is tracking along really nicely.” An artist’s impression of the $1.5 billion Teneriffe Banks development. Kokoda Property Group The spokesperson added that the first stage of development remained on track for 2028, with construction to begin late this year or early 2027. But a buyer who put forward a 10 per cent deposit on a $4.8 million three-bedroom apartment in the complex in late 2024 said communication had not been good enough, and anything that could delay construction was a significant concern due to a sunset clause in her contract. The clause could allow the developer to terminate its sale agreement and refund her deposit if construction criteria weren’t met within 3½ years of the deal being signed.





A second buyer at Teneriffe Banks said they were not overly concerned by recent developments, and believed their apartment would be delivered. The Kokoda spokesperson added that the sprawling marina shown in marketing material would absolutely be built as pictured, despite questions previously being raised about its approval process. World.title: Over 100 olympic pools of ‘bin juice’ from this Perth tip is seeping into the ground
World.content:
NationalWAWaste Over 100 olympic pools of ‘bin juice’ from this Perth tip is seeping into the ground Alastair Kirkby Indigo Lemay-Conway and August 19, 2026 — 8:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There is no secret that the smell from a landfill stinks. But the real concern is what is beneath the surface. At Tamala Park Waste Facility, situated in Perth’s northern suburbs, the answer to that is leachate, and a lot of it. Tamala Park opened in 1991. Mindarie Regional Council Tamala Park landfill is run by the Mindarie Regional Council and has accepted the household waste of 800,000 Perth homes for 35 years. The council is made up of seven local governments and was due to reach the end of its operational life around 2028, however, an excessive buildup of liquid waste is now threatening to derail those closure plans.



As of October 2024, data shows there were 167 olympic sized swimming pools worth of leachate accumulated at the bottom of the tip. Without any removal methods in place, that number is expected to have risen. The situation has now triggered formal regulatory enforcement. Western Australia’s Department of Water and Environmental Regulation issued the regional council an official Environmental Protection Notice on August 3. The notice requires the MRC to provide a detailed and accurate determination of the leachate levels as well as a leachate removal plan, and they have 30 days to do it. The EPN also requires the council to improve its landfill gas management, provide updated landfill closure planning, and undertake additional technical investigations. Western Sydney University science professor Ian Wright has been a water scientist for 30 years and describes leachate as the liquid often seen at the bottom of household bins.



“Leachate is the liquid that builds up in rotting rubbish. So a lot of people might have seen it if your garbage bin with lots of food and kitchen scraps has been left in the house, and you perhaps went away for a few days,” he said. Western Sydney University science professor Ian Wright. “It’s often a tea-coloured liquid that stinks, and it’s basically decomposing waste, and it’s chemically full of lots and lots of contaminants.” Wright said the 167 olympic pools worth of leachate was a significant amount to be accumulated at the bottom of any tip and that it was “a major issue” for groundwater health. The landfill is only partially lined and the MRC’s recent request to install a piggyback liner and create a leachate management area in the northern portion of the tip – closest to the nearby residential homes – was rejected by DWER at the beginning of August.



A DWER spokesperson said the high leachate levels was one of the reasons behind the decision. “Highly elevated leachate levels were a significant consideration during the assessment of a piggyback liner and leachate management area,” they said. “Following detailed technical assessment, DWER concluded that the proposed works would generate additional leachate and would not adequately address the existing leachate, odour and groundwater issues at the site.” The regulatory body also acknowledged there are ongoing investigations into groundwater contamination at the site but that there is currently a “low” risk to human health and the broader environment. Wright said he was “very surprised” the landfill hadn’t been fully lined as to prevent groundwater contamination of the nearby Gnangara aquifer, which provides almost half of all the water used in the Perth metropolitan area each year.



“As soon as I heard about this case study, my mind went straight to: could this be in any way a threat or a risk to Perth’s groundwater? Because the Gnangara sand aquifer is right on the edge of this area,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Waste Plans trashed: Where to dump one-third of Perth’s household waste? “It’s easy for waste from something like this landfill to move through sand down to the aquifer, so as to contaminate the groundwater.” Wright said groundwater contamination wasn’t the only risk associated with leachate buildup as methane can also be a byproduct of the breakdown of household waste. “With all this rotting landfill, and particularly the organic wastes that start breaking down, because it’s sealed under metres and metres of landfill, it starts breaking down away from oxygen, and that can create the perfect environment for methane,” he said.



Methane presents a threefold-hazard for Wright: it’s a bad greenhouse gas, it stinks, and it’s explosive. “The thing with methane is it stinks. There are suburbs growing around here, and I’m actually very surprised there isn’t a larger buffer around this landfill for the suburban development,” he said. “Methane can also blow up, and one of the concerns in the auditor’s report is that it is an explosive gas, and the gas coming from this rotting waste underground can actually rise through the surface, through the layers of soil and landfill, and if there are buildings nearby, it can sometimes rise into them. “It can even go through concrete slabs, concrete is a porous material. It can build up in buildings, and yes, it can build up to explosive levels.” Wright said he would encourage the MRC to embrace the residents and their concerns around the leachate.



“Outrage can ferment with something like this,” he said. Resident Mary O’Byrne has been championing the odour issue at Tamala Park for years and is now calling on government officials to step in. “My concern is the groundwater, what’s happening to that, and how it affects residents,” she said. “I want a government inquiry into how this place is run. I want to know why, for three and a half years, they didn’t evaporate the leachate.” Mary O’Byrne is a resident who has been campaigning against the odour and environmental concerns at Tamala Park Waste Facility. 9 News Perth



Wright said he felt like the council was trying to do their best to mitigate the problems that likely began long before most councillors were in their roles. “I can see that the council is trying their absolute best to take account of all those decisions in the past, and manage it best for locals, but there’s lots of challenges here,” he said. A spokesperson for the MRC said they were taking the management of the landfill and the protection of the surrounding environment “extremely seriously”. “Elevated levels of leachate within the landfill is an issue that both MRC and the regulator have been aware of for some time. We share DWER’s concerns on this matter and are committed to finding a viable and lasting solution,” they said. “MRC presented this information to the regulator voluntarily, and we have worked with the Department for several years to monitor and manage the site’s environmental risks and to ensure the landfill can be safely and successfully rehabilitated.”



But they said they couldn’t quantify the amount of leachate contained within the landfill and that it was a focus of their work in the coming months. “We continue to deploy measures on site to control the amount of leachate generated, to prioritise the capping of open landfill areas, and to optimise odour management.” Wright warns however that it will take many decades to manage the leachate issues on the site. “Grandchildren of people living in this area will still have to deal with this,” he said.

World.title: Urgent debate or urgent farewell: MPs discuss Chris Penk
World.content:
Tuesday's urgent parliamentary debate on Chris Penk's demotion was about a fairly specific topic: the prime minister's decision to remove one of his ministers from Cabinet for disloyalty. In practice, it was a rather more eclectic collection of reckons from around the House. At times it resembled a fond farewell tribute.

Urgent debate or urgent farewell: MPs debate demotion of Chris Penk The House Download MP3 5m

There was the expected political crossfire over the events of the previous week. Labour argued it exposed deeper problems for Christopher Luxon's leadership. National MPs' responses were tantamount to "nothing to see here", instead aiming to spotlight Labour's hypothetical tax policies. But there were also more personal interpretations of the situation.

ACT's Simon Court used a decent portion of his contribution to lament the end of Penk's ministerial tenure, and praise Penk's work in the Building and Construction portfolio. He tucked in some campaigning too. Court is standing in Penk's electorate and hoping some of Penk's supporters might jump into the ACT waka instead of the National one as a protest or proxy vote.

Simon Court praises Chris Penk and then makes a plea for voters to choose him as Penk's replacement during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk. VNP / Phil Smith

Court's praise contrasted with the political argument surrounding Penk's removal. At times the debate sounded less like a dispute over a ministerial decision and more like a valedictory for someone who had already left.

Te Pāti Māori's Debbie Ngarewa-Packer and Labour's Carmel Sepuloni both went out of their way to acknowledge the now former minister personally, describing him in warm terms as an "honourable man" who was "here for the right reasons", and praising the way he conducted himself across the House.

Te Pāti Māori leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Te Pāti Māori's Debbie Ngarewa-Packer described Penk as "one of the better human beings on that side".

Former National Party leader Judith Collins appears to enjoy an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Almost the only party not to praise the fallen minister was his own party. As speeches ping-ponged back and forth between the two major parties, the very short contributions from National MPs largely stuck to the party line: Penk acted alone, actions have consequences, and it was time to move on.

Then there was Kieran McAnulty, who praised Penk but focused on picking apart attempts by various National MPs to draw a line under the events.

Kieran McAnulty dissects the Prime Minister's sacking from cabinet of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge. VNP / Phil Smith

Through all of this, there were two notable absences - both the demoter and the demoted.

Christopher Luxon's seat remains empty during an urgent debate into the Prime Minister's sacking of Chris Penk for fronting a leadership challenge against him. VNP / Phil Smith

Chris Penk isn't at Parliament this week, and was not in the House to explain his actions, or respond to the various assessments of his character and political judgment. The prime minister had departed the House prior to the end of Question Time; his actions as well as Penk's were debated without him. The one minister present who was discussed was Erica Stanford, who sat still and silent, like a pupil sent to await the headmaster.

Ultimately, the House's traversal of last week's political melodrama was a forum for criticism, defence, campaigning and a fond farewell from the most unexpected quarters, missing only its protagonists.

World.title: Winter illnesses harming students' education, NZPF president says
World.content:
The principal of a Napier kura says more than half of their students are not at school this week because they are sick.

Maraenui Bilingual School Tumuaki, Traci Liddall, said 67 percent of their 125 students stayed home on Monday, and 56 percent did on Tuesday and Wednesday. All but two of those students were reported to have flu-like symptoms.

Data from the Ministry of Education showed almost 10 percent of class time was lost across the country last week due to illness. The past couple of weeks have been the worst in three years for school absences due to illness and medical reasons.

Hawke's Bay has been hit hard - one day last week, Napier Girl's High had 20 percent of its students, or about 200 girls, off due to sickness. The Terrace School - a primary in Waikpukurau - had 76 kids off on Tuesday, about a third of its roll, as well as six teachers.

Liddall said the Ministry of Education advising parents to send children to school with mild symptoms like a runny nose was unhelpful.

"It bothers me that the ministry are on our back about attendance, but we can't help this.

"As much as we would like the tamariki to be at kura, I'd rather sick kids stay at home and get properly well before they come to school, otherwise they just spread germs.

"Sending kids with sniffles is not a good message to be sending, so I'm disappointed to see that."

She said three teachers at the bilingual school, including herself, were also sick.

They had merged some classes, but they often did that due to small class numbers, to give teachers relief time.

Liddal said she had not seen sickness-related absences this high in her 30-year teaching career, other than during Covid-19.

"Fifteen to 20 percent would be a bad day for absences for us, unless there's something going on in the community, like a big tangi.

"I've never seen anything like this."

Winter illnesses are harming students' education, the president of the New Zealand Principals' Federation says.

Have you been affected by school sickness? Get in touch at iwitness@rnz.co.nz

NZPF president Jason Miles said absences that high affected student learning.

"You've got to work out what the children have missed in that time that they've been away. It's about the teachers knowing their children, knowing what they have missed and looking at what they can do to catch up," he told RNZ.

The principal's federation encouraged children to stay away if they were unwell, but to come back as soon as they were feeling better, he said.

"There are different communities that are hit harder than others for a period of time, and it takes 5-10 days to get over this flu, so in that time you've got a number of children who are sick, a number of children who about to get sick and of course you've got staff who are sick as well."

Illness among staff was particularly problematic, and was putting huge pressure on the relieving teacher pool, particularly in high schools.

"When you've got a lot of children away, it's fairly straightforward, but if you've got more staff away, percentage-wise, than children, then that's a really difficult space for leaders to be in, because that's about getting enough adults to keep your school open.

"So school leaders are either having to double up classes, put management staff in classes, which impacts on other parts of running the school, or rostering some years home."

The Ministry of Education said it shared guidance published by Health New Zealand on its website to support parents in deciding whether their child was well enough to attend school.

"We know parents are often making these decisions first thing in the morning, and it isn't always clear-cut," group general manager Helen Hurst said.

"When symptoms are mild, it may not always be obvious whether a child needs to stay home. The guidance helps parents make that call.

"Regular attendance is important for learning, but children who are sick should stay home. When they are well enough to learn, they should be at school."

Auckland Primary Principals' Association executive Lucy Naylor told the NZ Herald that parents could not afford to have a "she'll be right attitude" towards illness.

She acknowledged there could be "conflicting messaging" over when to keep children home, however.

Health NZ has official guidance for when children should not be at school.

It states: "If a child is too unwell to learn or they have an infectious illness that could spread easily to others, they need to be kept at home away from school so they can recover or get health advice or care."

World.title: Airbnb crisis or economic boom? Methven grapples with housing tensions
World.content:
Julianne is new to Methven, a ski town with a decidedly provincial vibe about an hour from Christchurch.

She has not lived there for long but has noticed a topic on almost everyone's lips.

"I'm just trying to buy a house and a lot of the houses are going for an extremely higher price because they're going into Airbnbs rather than for the people that live here," she says.

Housing affordability is an issue many will grumble about quietly but few are willing to put their names or faces to the complaints.

Crossroads run through the heart of Methven, an apt metaphor for the problem striking at the heart of the community.

Average property values rose by almost 70 percent from 2018 to 2024, climbing from $380,000 to $640,000.

The latest census figures show more than 13 percent of the town's homes are unoccupied.

Ashburton District Council estimates 130 to 170 Airbnbs and other short-term lets are operating in Methven, which has fewer than 1000 homes, although the council admits the figures are just an estimate.

A cursory search on the Airbnb platform shows more than 200 options for a short-term stay in the town.

New homes in Methven. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Methven home-owner Paul Dixey says his neighbourhood and the town's identity are changing for the worse.

"We're finding a lot of - not that I've got anything against people outside of Methven - but there are a lot of people outside of Methven taking advantage of the housing market here, procuring houses, not actually living here, but putting them up as accommodation houses, particularly Airbnbs," he says.

"We've got nothing against the small Airbnbs which the council allow in a 'residential c' environment, but we're against the big ones that are taking in 10 to 12, 15 people, which we believe are just really commercial entities. To a certain extent, they're invading the residential suburbs of Methven and that's putting pressure on the housing market."

Methven locals pushed off of property ladder by Airbnbs Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The council's group manager compliance and development Ian Hyde says residential zoning rules are part of the reason staff can only estimate the number of short-term lets in Methven.

"Within residential zones short-term lets are permitted for up to a maximum of five guests per night and in rural zones 10 is allowed," he says.

"If within those rules, no neighbour's approval or registration with council is needed. Anything beyond those numbers is generally considered a discretionary activity and requires a land use consent."

If people offering short-term rentals stuck to those numbers and the council stuck to its zoning rules, Dixey believes there would be fewer problems.

"If you look at our little street here, Glennifer, I'm guessing there are probably 15, 20 houses in this wee street, probably four of them are Airbnbs," he says.

"There would be more if the permanent residents hadn't clamped down a bit.

"We've had one here that got resource consent to have 12 or more people and immediately the house across the road applied for the same. Luckily the neighbours either side of it objected and it didn't pass but according to council everyone in the street could apply and virtually the whole street could become Airbnb."

The council's group manager compliance and development says residential zoning rules are part of the reason staff can only estimate the number of short-term lets in Methven. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Signs of permanent suburban hotels

Dixey is not opposed to people letting their home out for a weekend while they are away but sees signs that homes are being used as a kind of permanent suburban hotel.

In the streets nearby about two dozen homes show up on Airbnb, with house rules hanging up through street-facing windows.

"Any houses here around that $800,000 to $900,000 - that seems to be the bracket that is selling the best here - a lot of those are being bought up as Airbnbs or accommodation houses," Dixey says.

"That obviously squeezes the people who are looking to buy a permanent house to live in."

Dixey says he has noticed a trend of people building commercial-type accommodation and retroactively applying for consent to allow the homes to be used that way.

He believes most of the owners live out of the town, with some using the homes during the ski season.

Most locals are reticent to talk about Airbnb and short-term letting, lest they cause upset in the tight-knit town, but those who will share a quick and quiet opinion with RNZ express concern an abundance of short-term lets is pushing up prices and squeezing renters out.

Methven Community Board chairperson Megan Fitzgerald RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Avoiding 'a ghost town'

Methven Community Board chairperson Megan Fitzgerald says authorities have to strike a balance.

"Everyone is in agreement that we can't have a ghost town," she says.

"We need to have our residents here as part of our community but we also can't stifle that economic growth."

So is Methven destined to become Canterbury's answer to Queenstown or Arrowtown?

"You can see it kind of around town that there are a few more houses but also now you drive around town and when traditionally it would have been quiet and empty, actually now you're walking down streets with tourists, people that you can clearly tell are visiting our town for the weekend and that's awesome," Fitzgerald says.

"You go on to those booking websites and you try and find accommodation in Methven and it's often booked out and that means that there's people here in our town filling the gaps. It's not unoccupied."

With plenty of cash flowing into places like Arrowtown and Queenstown, Fitzgerald says that must not come at the cost of the community.

"You could have them spending money in the cafes but only two business owners that don't have a functioning school for the kids to go to," she says.

"A community is more than just money coming in and that's where I come back to the residents. The residents are the heart of the community but we also need money coming in so it's a balancing act. It's an equilibrium. It's finding that middle ground for the community."

Short-term letting also creates tension with traditional commercial accommodation businesses.

Warren Nisbet, who is the owner of Methven Motels and Apartments. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Motels, hotels counting cost

Methven Motels and Apartments owner Warren Nisbet says motels and hotels are at a disadvantage because of compliance and overhead costs.

"All these people that are sucking that money out of our community and it's mainly not locals, it's mainly from outsiders. They're taking advantage of it and they should be paying the compliance costs as we do," he says.

"Building warrant of fitness, the fire service come once a year, we have a monthly check of our fire alarms, and probably the Airbnbs haven't got a fire exit plan as such, which we've got to produce every year and upgrade it if necessary."

James McKenzie, Mt Hutt Ski Area manager and project director RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Seeing the positives

Mt Hutt Ski Area manager James McKenzie sees the positive side and believes initial fears about a glut of Airbnbs may have been overstated.

"I don't think it's shifted that much," he says.

"Methven's got a really special character. It's the sort of town where you walk along the street and you still stop to chat to people, people wave as they drive down the street. It's a very courteous, very small community.

"The likes of the hot pools manage capacity so that it's not overrun, there's a certain amount of capacity each day, it means that we're not overwhelming the town. Those who potentially had some concerns have certainly I've heard come back from that position to say 'actually, it's not what we thought it would be, it's actually being really well managed, we're not being overrun, we're not being overwhelmed'.

"The services in town are improving, the quality of the accommodation base, the housing stock is improving, it's still affordable, we've still got nice people walking around town. It hasn't become this sort of tourist mecca hub where we're just overwhelmed and finding that we haven't got the adequate infrastructure to deal with it.

"I think we're a long way from that point. I just get that sense that we won't really get there because there's still such a massive draw to Southern Lakes and Otago and the cities. That means the places like Methven will remain pretty special into the longer term."

The Mt Hutt skifield. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Short-term lets have opened the town to more visitors with different budgets, McKenzie says.

"Methven is certainly a growing town and the old hotel model is hard to sustain, certainly in a place like Methven where you don't get that year-round continuity of business," he says.

"With people investing into town and buying Airbnbs there is now a bed base that people can come to and the quality accommodation has come up as a result of that increased bed base. It is easy for people to choose Methven as a destination now with the slightly older hotel accommodation still there, but now there's sort of another level of more premium accommodation in town, which is really good for us on the ski field and for the other activity providers in town."

Dixey wants an even playing field for commercial operators and says the council needs to step up and enforce its existing rules so the town can get back some balance.

New housing in the Mid Canterbury town. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Fitzgerald says she has sympathy for commercial operators and for people living in subdivisions where Airbnbs keep springing up.

She says the community board is working with the council to make sure it gets its policies right and while housing is causing some friction in town, so far tempers are in check.

"There are always going to be differing views. Someone said to me once, 'the best policy that you can create is one that no one loves but everyone can agree to'. I think that's really important to keep in mind, we're not going to find a silver bullet.

World.title: Hawke's Bay Coffin Club searches for new home amid struggles to meet demand
World.content:
The Hawke's Bay Coffin Club donates hundreds of baby coffins to hospitals every year, but can't keep up with demand, because the group doesn't have a permanent space of its own.

The club is run entirely by volunteers and anyone can become a member, which then means they can buy and design their own personalised coffin.

The group of about 40 members are mostly elderly and retired, and gather every Tuesday morning at an old sports building in Hastings to make coffins.

Hawke's Bay Coffin Club searches for new home Morning Report Download MP3 4m

However, a growing part of the charity's work is in making baby coffins, funded through the adult coffin purchases. In the past financial year, volunteers have made and donated more than 500 baby coffins, valued at more than $175,000.

"That's a huge amount for our little club and it just shows the need that is out there in society," said club treasurer Cherie Hames.

From talking to hospitals, she believes their club is the only group in New Zealand making this many baby coffins, but despite hospitals and birthing units needing more, they aren't able to meet that demand.

"We are at a point where we don't have the room to make any more," Hames said. "We are basically at capacity of what we can make on the premises, we have to find new premises."

Volunteer Pete Wolstenholme holding one of the baby coffins, which contain a hand-knitted blanket and teddy bear made by local ladies. RNZ/Alexa Cook

The baby coffins are stored in a little room out the back of the main workshop, and inside each coffin lies a hand-knitted cuddly bear and blanket crafted by local ladies.

"It's devastating," said volunteer Alan Monk. "You can imagine a family expecting a newborn and, all of a sudden, it's all over.

"That's the last thing, the absolute last thing on the list that they would have even considered they had to get ready."

The baby coffins are currently being made next to the club's main workshop, in an old cold netball ablution block, where rusty cobweb-covered showerheads still stick out of the concrete walls.

Don Mardle oversees the production of hundreds of baby coffins. RNZ/Alexa Cook

Volunteer Don Mardle oversees the operation, which he said could produce more coffins, if they had a larger building and more volunteers.

"We're restricted by space and labour," he said. "This year, we are up to 147 as of today and that's only scratching the surface really.

"I'm a retired tradie, I came here to make adult coffins, but found my space making baby coffins."

Mardle volunteers more than 20 hours a week of labour to ensure enough baby coffins are made.

"It's an incredible privilege to be doing this," he said. "I love giving to our community and, if there are any tradies out there - joiners, cabinet makers - we'd love some help," he said.

Hames said people volunteer from all walks of life and for all sorts of reasons.

"Some of the women have had miscarriages in the past and the way that was dealt with was not the nicest, so for them, it fills a real need," he said.

"On the other side of it too, we have people that are in resthomes that are still useful. Just because you go into a rest home, doesn't mean there isn't an area you can fill.

"I don't think volunteering and usefulness stops at a certain age."

Dave Beal gluing together the lid for a baby coffin. RNZ/Alexa Cook

For the past 11 years, the Coffin Club has leased its buildings off the Hastings District Council on a six-month rolling contract.

The council told RNZ the area had not been earmarked for any particular activity or development to date.

"Decisions on its future will be made by council in consultation with the community, once strategic planning work being undertaken for Windsor Park, including Splash Planet, is completed and as resources allow," a spokesperson said.

"Given that the future of the green space is undecided, council will not approve new buildings on it."

The council said any club or organisation wishing to establish premises on council-owned land may submit an application, and it had not received an application from the Coffin Club.

Hames said the club was worried it would have to move, once a decision was made about the future of Windsor Park, so the group was hunting for land in Hastings to build a permanent home and continue the club's legacy.

"We need to be somewhere we can expand and build, or alter to fit our purposes.

"Anybody willing to help donate and get us to our goal, we would really appreciate that. We are a worthwhile cause."

Hawke's Bay Coffin Club Treasurer is worried about the charity's future and hoping they can find some land and funding to continue building coffins. RNZ/Alexa Cook

'We have a lot of fun here'

Volunteer Pete Wolstenholme joined the club more than three years ago, although he's yet to make his own coffin.

"When I retired, I needed something to do," he said. "I saw it advertised and thought, 'That sounds different, I'll go down and have a look'.

"I had the thought that probably a lot of people have, that it's a bit morbid, but it's far from it. We have a lot of fun here, we're always laughing."

Pete's friend, Alan Monk, has also volunteered for several years, helping many people design their final resting place. He said Kiwis attitude toward death was evolving.

"More and more, there is an acceptance that I've got to get ready for that day, it's going to come sometime, so I've got to help my family by putting things together.

"People sort of say, 'Well, that's my final bed', so we talk about this as 'underground furniture'," Monk said.

For some, it's an opportunity to have a bit of fun decorating their coffin. Wolstenholme and Monk laugh, as they remember one member who turned his coffin into a truck.

"He was a heavy truck driver and his coffin had big lights on the front, it had a sound-effect motor in it and lights actually working," Monk said.

The friends enjoyed the camaraderie that came with being part of the club and the sense of purpose in giving back, which Hames said was a common feeling among members.

World.title: Flu wards set up, elective surgery cancelled as hospital admissions surge
World.content:
Influenza spike sees Covid-style measures return Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Hospitals have created dedicated flu wards and some elective surgery is being cancelled, as influenza A hits the health system hard.

Health bosses were now meeting daily to monitor the situation and keep an eye on hospital capacity across the country, with the upper North Island most affected.

Nurses said Health NZ was not doing enough and front-line health staff were struggling to cope.

Over the past two weeks, the number of patients turning up to emergency departments had increased and, in the first week of August, flu admissions doubled.

Health NZ winter planning lead Chris Lowry said flu-only wards helped keep others safe.

"If we aggregate people together, that helps stop any internal spread, when you might have them scattered through a ward... even if they are in isolation."

She was not able to name all the hospitals that had dedicated flu wards, but said they tended to be larger hospitals.

Health NZ winter planning lead Chris Lowry said flu-only wards helped keep others safe. RNZ

As well as the daily meeting, Health NZ had set up a national co-ordination centre to help with planning and support any areas that needed it , Lowry said.

Each hospital had 'flex beds' that could move to where they were most needed, as part of Health NZ's winter plan, released in April with a promise to help ease pressure, but the NZ Nurses Organisation is asking where that plan is.

Delegate and Waikato Hospital emergency department nurse Tracy Chisholm said there was very little sign of it - including the extra beds.

'Bed block' - where patients became stuck in the emergency department, because there was no space for them in a hospital ward - was still happening, she said. That contributed to regular wait-times of 10 hours or more.

Lowry said the planned flex beds were not always available, partly because winter illness was also taking out the nurses who would staff them, but the union said Health NZ should have addressed chronic understaffing.

A really 'yuck' strain

Many general practices were also separating patients with flu-like symptoms.

NZ College of General Practitioners president Luke Bradford said some were holding dedicated respiratory clinics or seeing patients with flu symptoms in a different space to others.

NZ College of General Practitioners president Luke Bradford is taking his own advice this week, because of flu-like symptoms. Supplied

Those who ended up in hospital tended to have either developed secondary infections, such as pneumonia, had complicating conditions, or were unwell from high fevers or dehydration, he said.

"Every so often, you get a strain of flu that is just yuck, that does makes people feel particularly unwell, and I think that's what we've got this year. It does seem to have come quickly, as the peak's ramped up very fast."

Doctors at the top of the North Island had particularly noticed big numbers through the doors, with the peak appearing to hit later than the South Island, he said.

Bradford was following his own advice this week, staying home and away from a planned gathering, because of flu-like symptoms.

"I wrote myself a list of chores and then have failed to get any of them done, so I've actually sat on the sofa with some Panadol and fluids and a cup of tea, and been watching some streaming programmes," he said

Anyone with flu should rest and hydrate, and contact their doctor, if they were worried, or had shortness of breath, chest pain, a worsening fever or felt very unwell.

Lowry said anyone who needed to go to an emergency department should always go, and they would be seen and well cared for.

World.title: Arthur's Pass campsite torn up by 4WD vehicles
World.content:
The Department of Conservation (DOC) is appealing to the public for help after a popular campsite at Arthur's Pass in the South Island was torn up by 4WD vehicles.

The popular and picturesque Klondyke Corner Campsite draws thousands of visitors each year and was a key feature of the annual Coast to Coast multi-sport race.

Aerial photos illustrate the extend of damage which was believed to have happened on 1 August at about 4pm.

An aerial view of damage from four-wheel drive vehicles at Klondyke Corner Campsite in Arthur's Pass. Supplied / Department of Conservation

DOC operations manager Leeann Ellis said it was incredibly disappointing.

"The vehicles have left deep tyre tracks over a large area, compacting the soil, creating wide ruts and making the site much more susceptible to erosion in heavy rain," she said.

"They have also destroyed plants and opened the area up for weeds to grow and take over. Its ruined what was a fantastic place and created the potential for a muddy mess in heavy rain."

The department was working with police to try and identify the vehicles and said it welcomed any information from the public.

An aerial view of damage from four-wheel drive vehicles at Klondyke Corner Campsite in Arthur's Pass. Supplied / Department of Conservation

It was illegal to damage any national park's natural or historic features and to drive vehicles on off-formed roads.

Offenders can face heavy penalties, including infringement fines and prosecution.

Under the National Parks Act, interfering with or damaging a historic feature in a national park carried a maximum penalty for an individual of up to one year in prison, a $100,000 fine, or both.

"We appreciate four-wheel driving is an increasingly popular recreational activity," Ellis said.

"There are some fantastic tracks where drivers can challenge their skills and access some beautiful locations like the Edwards Valley and Maling Pass 4WD tracks in the St James Conservation Area. Our plea is don't go off road and cause damage to areas which are protected for a reason.

World.title: Controversial development plan for Pegasus Golf Course declined fast-track approval
World.content:
The Minister for Infrastructure has declined to refer a controversial plan to rip up Canterbury's Pegasus Golf Course for fast-track approval.

The property developer Wolfbrook bought the 18-hole course in May and planned to redevelop the land into 1000 homes and a mixed-use commercial and community area

A decision released on Wednesday on the Fast Track website said the Minister for Infrastructure Chris Bishop was not referring the project to the fast-track.

It said if a project was not referred, the applicant may apply for referral again.

"This is considered a new application, subject to fees and charges."

In its notice of decisions letter, Fast Track said the project could only be accepted if the minister was satisfied the criteria in section 22 was met, which included "'being satisfied the project was an infrastructure or development project that would have significant regional or national benefits."

"...and referring the project to the fast-track approvals process would facilitate the project, including by enabling it to be processed in a more timely and cost-effective way than under normal processes and is unlikely to materially affect the efficient operation of the fast-track approvals process.

"Additionally, the minister has the discretion to decline a referral application for any other reason, whether or not the project meets the criteria in section 22 of the Act," it said.

World.title: Gisborne slash clash: Mayor feels like 'meat in the middle'
World.content:
Gisborne Mayor Rehette Stoltz says she feels like the ''meat in the middle'' between her community and the forestry sector.

Forestry Minister Todd McClay had told the Gisborne District Council that its approach to sediment management and forestry slash was too tough and a facilitator had been appointed to help "reset the relationship" with the sector.

Stoltz told Checkpoint that a meeting with the minister on Wednesday had been "productive" and the Gisborne community deserved a "collaborative" approach between local and central government.

Gisborne mayor meets with Forestry minister over approach to 'slash' Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

She said community members told her that the council's approach to consent was not tough enough, but that the forestry industry had expressed a different view.

"We are getting constant feedback that it is strict, or that the industry is finding that the consent conditions are stricter than what they would expect, so, what we then said is 'We are doing our work, but we hear you'. So we are going to ask an independent panel to evaluate what we have in our consenting regime, how we plan and is it proportionate to the risk we are trying to look after?"

Stoltz said the council had appointed an independent reviewer - Chris Finlayson - to look at its consent conditions.

"I feel sometimes like the meat in the middle, where we are trying to look after our environment, we are trying to make sure there is economic activity as well. So, from one side we are hearing 'it feels like this is too tough'. Our community are feeding back to us saying ít's not tough enough. So we are testing that, because at the end of the day we do want to make sure it is fit for purpose and that's exactly what we are doing now."

Stoltz said following Cyclone Gabrielle the government appointed a panel to investigate the impact of storm damage caused by wood debris and sediment on communities.

World.title: Ikitau back in fray as Wallabies eye Argentina tour
World.content:
Les Kiss has resisted throwing any curveballs ahead of the Wallabies' tour of Argentina, with a fit Len Ikitau the only addition to the squad that produced wins in his first two Tests as coach.

Ikitau (ankle), the 2025 Wallabies player of the year, had minor surgery and missed the recent victories against Japan in Osaka and Townsville.

He has effectively replaced unlucky fullback Jock Campbell, who impressed in the number 15 jersey against Ireland before injuries elsewhere saw him employed as a play-making bench option against France.

With Tom Wright locked in at fullback, Campbell, who was named the Queensland Reds' best player at this week's end-of-season awards, was replaced by Ben Donaldson as the fullback or fly half bench cover for the next three Tests.

Les Kiss seeking pride The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Centre Josh Flook has also been left out while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (hamstring) will also return after missing Saturday's Townsville Test, creating a log-jam of midfield options against the world number seven Pumas.

Winger Max Jorgensen has been included despite coming off with a sore chest on Saturday, while code-hopper Zac Lomax remains on the injury list and unavailable for selection.

Lock Miles Amatosero, unavailable for the first Test as part of a three-game suspension for a red card earned in Osaka, was also not considered for selection.

Kiss, who tested new combinations in the pack and centres in his first two games in charge, has otherwise played a straight bat ahead of what will be sterner tests in San Salvador de Jujuy and Mendoza on August 30 and September 6.

"As coaches, we've looked to maintain consistency in selection, with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks through their hard work and connection on and off the field," he said.

"Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it's one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game."

Where Kiss selects Suaalii will be telling after Isaac Henry's strong running and second-phase play at outside centre caught the eye in Townsville.

Hunter Paisami has also impressed at number 12 in Ikitau's absence, leading to questions post-match about where Suaalii fits in the picture.

There is a push for former NRL star Suaalii to move to the wing to ensure more involvement and better harness his aerial ability.

Kiss, who replaced Joe Schmidt ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup, said before his first Test in charge that he was "persisting at number 13 with him at this stage, but I know that he can go to fullback and wing, and that's important to acknowledge as well".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But Campbell and Flook's exclusion from this squad hints that Kiss is now considering a Suaalii switch.

Zane Nonggorr (calf) remains sidelined, with Massimo De Lutiis set for his first full Wallabies tour after arriving late into Osaka and debuting in Townsville.

Wright will notch 50 Test caps if he plays in both Tests.

The squad will assemble in Sydney on Saturday, before departing for Buenos Aires on Sunday.

WALLABIES SQUAD: Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Massimo de Lutiis, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw , Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (c), Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Dylan Pietsch, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

World.title: Germany star says neurological issue behind two collapses in a week
World.content:
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has revealed a neurological issue but says he is doing well despite collapsing during a preseason game for the second time in a week.

The 23-year-old Germany international went down shortly after entering Wednesday's (AEST) friendly as a substitute in the second half. Players from both teams made a circle around Musiala as he received medical treatment. He was then helped as he walked off the pitch.

Musiala had collapsed Sunday (AEST) during a friendly against Leipzig. German news agency DPA reported he had left the field on his own but still appeared dazed.

After Wednesday's game, Musiala posted a message on his Instagram account, explaining that he had been diagnosed with temporary "but easily treatable absence seizures" caused by a neurological problem.

"These can lead to the moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or even now in Heidenheim," Musiala wrote.

Bayern, in its report on Wednesday's game, only said of the incident: "There was a setback when Jamal Musiala had to be subbed off with a knock minutes after coming on."

Jamal Musiala was held up by teammate Ismael Saibari (left) after fainting during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Musiala said he was "very optimistic" and was receiving excellent medical treatment.

"The important thing is that there is no additional health risk," he wrote.

"In close coordination and regular communication with experts, it has been my personal wish to face the challenge and, with the endorsement of the neurological specialists, to devote myself to what helps me most in recovery: to simply live my everyday life and keep up with my passion of playing football," Musiala added.

Bundesliga champion Bayern faces Borussia Dortmund on Sunday AEST in the German Supercup, the traditional curtain-raiser for the season.

AP

World.title: Irankunda says Hanson's monoculture comments upset team during World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos star winger Nestory Irankunda says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's comments on multiculturalism upset many of the players during the recent World Cup.

The Australian team was competing at the tournament in North America in June when Ms Hanson made a speech at the National Press Club saying Australia should end its policy of multiculturalism in favour of a monoculture.

"It really did upset me and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that," Irankunda said.

" I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it. "

Irankunda, who is one of several Socceroos players from a refugee background, told 702 ABC Sydney while he tried to stay off social media it was hard to avoid the senator's comments.

Loading...

"There can be some people who do the wrong thing but that doesn't mean that's all of us," he said.

"There's people like me, and Awer [Mabil], Mohamed Touré that go out there. There's a lot of boys like us that go out there and do the right thing.

"I don't like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people who do bad."

Irankunda was born in a refugee camp in Tanzania in 2006 to Burundian parents who fled the nation's civil war. He came to Australia when he was three months old.

Irankunda was speaking with presenter Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney just days after moving from English Championship club Watford to Portuguese side Sporting CP for an undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million.

The footballer said he probably wouldn't like to speak with the One Nation senator as he was still upset by the comments and "some of the things she said in the past".

"I'm not someone that likes to jump into controversial things or this political stuff. But I mean, you know, you never know," Irankunda said.

"One day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting to her. So I mean … we'll see what happens."

Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club included a call to end Australia's decades-old policy of multiculturalism. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

After her press club speech, Hanson said the Socceroos represented her vision of a monocultural Australia.

"People from different background and cultures and nations all wearing the green and gold and representing one nation under one flag and succeeding under the same set of rules," Hanson said in the Senate in June.

Socceroo Awer Mabil addressed the monoculture debate when he returned in July from the tournament, declaring his team was not distracted and that it was "all bullshit" to suggest Australia was not a multicultural society.

Australian team destined to 'go far'

Irankunda said despite the Round of 32 loss to Egypt, the Socceroos had youth on their side and could go further into the tournament.

"You can see now with the likes of Lucas Herrington, Ali [Alessandro] Circati, Jordy Bos, you know, Mohamed Touré, all these names, all these young boys coming through, including myself," Irankunda said.

"There's still a lot of talent coming through in Australia right now.

"Only time will tell how far we can go. But I feel like in my heart that we can go pretty far."

World.title: Victorian detectives to head to NSW as Swans hotel investigation expands
World.content:
Victorian sex crime detectives are expected to travel to New South Wales as they investigate an alleged sex assault scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans.

The ABC understands the investigation centres on an allegation of touching without consent at the Pullman Hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is understood the alleged victim has spoken to police.

Multiple law enforcement sources have told the ABC that four officers from the Victoria Police Sex Crimes Squad will land in Sydney as they expand their investigation.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges over the alleged incident.

Earlier today the Swans said their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending five star players proves how committed they are to upholding standards at the club.

The Swans suspended Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner for the remainder of the 2026 AFL season over an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

At least five players were linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault and none of the banned players have been formally interviewed by police, according to the club, or charged.

In addition to the club sanction, the five Swans players will not be considered for All Australian selection, according to the AFL.

"Following the decision and appropriate club sanction imposed by the Sydney Swans today in relation to the conduct of five of their players, the AFL has determined those players will not be considered for selection in the 2026 All Australian squad," the league said in a statement.

"This decision is independent of the ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The AFL said the 2026 All Australian squad would be finalised on Monday next week, with the team announced at the AFL Awards the next day in Melbourne.

Telstra has spoken out, saying it was "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney have been stood down. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

West Coast AFLW head coach Daisy Pearce has called on men to "be a good human" not just for themselves but for the effect they have on others. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt King)

AFLW pioneer Daisy Pearce says it is "disappointing" allegations of violence against women have arisen again in the AFL.

Speaking at a press conference, West Coast Eagles AFLW coach Pearce urged young men to consider how their behaviour impacted others.

"Be a good human. Be a good human and for those that are in high-profile positions understand that you being a good human matters but it also has a massive impact on what other people think is acceptable as well," she said.

"I'd just highlight that this breach of our standards relates to five players. So, there are many players who this doesn't apply to," he said. "However, clearly, when situations such as this emerge – and clearly, there has been a breakdown in standards – we will, in time – as a board, and as an executive team – we will review how we deal with these things going forward." Club to be in a 'better position going forward', Pridham says Pridham has taken a question about whether he believes the Swans' season is now "torpedoed". "I think you've always got to enter the field of play with the expectation of performing well," he said. He says the fact that the club is willing to ban "five of our absolute best players" from the rest of the season shows it's "not trying to brush anything under the carpet". "I'm confident that, having taken this action, we'll be in a better place going forward as a result of it," he said. Show more

World.title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
World.content:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.
